item.title: CAGE Code Lookup: 4 Steps to Find or Request One
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: CAGE code lookup made practical: search SAM.gov or DLA by name, trace codes from part numbers, and know when SAM assigns one or you request it from DLA.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To look up a CAGE code, search the company's legal name in SAM.gov's public Entity Information search. If the company isn't registered in SAM.gov, use DLA's CAGE Search & Inquiry at cage.dla.mil. If you need a CAGE code for your own business, you usually don't request one: when you register in SAM.gov, DLA's CAGE Branch assigns a code as part of the SAM registration process. A direct request at cage.dla.mil is only for U.S. offerors that don't otherwise register in SAM. Foreign firms get an NCAGE code through their national codification bureau or NSPA.

Which option is right for you?

Choose by what you're trying to do. Pick the first page from the table below. All of these official tools are free.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner: you need a CAGE code to bidSAM.gov entity registration (the CAGE code comes with it)SAM.gov → Get Started / Register Entity
You only need a CAGE for a non-SAM purpose (e.g., a procurement that doesn't require SAM)Direct request through DLAcage.dla.mil → request / update
Checking a teaming partner or subcontractorSAM.gov Entity Information search, then DLA to confirmSAM.gov Search
Daily work: checking vendors and partsDLA CAGE Search & Inquiry plus PUB LOG FLIS Searchcage.dla.mil and FLIS Data Electronic Reading Room
You have a part number, not a company namePUB LOG FLIS Search (public, free)PUB LOG
Foreign company (Australia, UK, Canada, etc.)NCAGE request through NSPA, routed to your national bureauNSPA ePortal
Limited budget, want free human helpYour local APEX Acceleratorapexaccelerators.us

The reasons, one line each:

  • Beginner: SAM registration is required to win most federal awards anyway, and it creates your CAGE code with no extra form.
  • Daily work use: DLA is where CAGE records live. SAM.gov only shows entities that registered and chose public display.
  • Budget: SAM.gov, cage.dla.mil, PUB LOG and NCAGE requests cost nothing. Paid "registration services" sell you something you can do yourself for free.

The 4-Step Decision Tree: Find It or Request It

Ask four questions in order. The first "yes" tells you which tool to use.

  1. Do you need your own code and plan to bid on federal contracts? Register in SAM.gov. Under FAR 52.204-16 (Aug 2020 version), offerors must provide a CAGE code with the offer, and it's "required prior to award." For U.S. entities, the CAGE Branch assigns it during SAM registration. Our SAM.gov Registration Guide: 7 Steps From UEI to Active covers each screen.
  2. Do you need your own code but won't register in SAM? The same FAR provision lets an offeror located in the U.S. or its outlying areas request one at cage.dla.mil "if registration in SAM is not required for the subject procurement."
  3. Are you a non-U.S. entity? FAR 52.204-16 sends foreign offerors to their country's NATO codification bureau, or to NSPA, for an NCAGE code.
  4. Are you looking up someone else's code? Start with the SAM.gov Entity Information search. Fall back to cage.dla.mil when the company isn't in SAM or has hidden its record. Use PUB LOG FLIS Search when all you have is a part number.

One more trigger: FAR 52.204-16 says that when FAR 52.204-17 or 52.212-3(p) requires CAGE codes for your immediate owner or highest-level owner, you must get those codes from the owner entities. Parent companies are where people most often get caught short at proposal time.

How to Look Up a CAGE Code by Company Name

Use SAM.gov's Entity Information search. It's public and needs no login. Enter the company's legal business name and the CAGE code shows on its public record. SAM.gov's public search shows registered entities with their CAGE code, UEI, address and registration status (Contractor/Vendor Guide: Finding My CAGE Code, PIEE).

Steps on SAM.gov

  1. Go to sam.gov and click Search in the top menu.
  2. In the domain selector on the left, choose Entity Information. The default domain is often Contract Opportunities, which won't return companies.
  3. Type the legal business name in the keyword box. Put it in quotes if the name contains common words.
  4. In the filters, keep both Active and Inactive registrations in view. A partner whose registration lapsed still has a CAGE code, and you want to know about the lapse.
  5. Open the matching record and read the CAGE/NCAGE field next to the Unique Entity ID.
  6. Check that the physical address matches the location you're dealing with. Each CAGE code identifies one legal entity at one location (DLA, via search summary of CAGE program pages).

Example

Say a prime contractor wants to add a small machining subcontractor called "Example Precision LLC." The prime searches the exact name and finds two records: one in Ohio, one in Texas. Each has its own CAGE code. The subcontract and the proposal's subcontractor list must use the code for the facility actually doing the work. (This is a hypothetical example. The point is that one company name can have several CAGE codes.)

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Searching a trade name. SAM indexes the legal business name, and DBA names don't always match. Fix: ask the partner for their UEI and search that instead.
  • No result at all. Registrants can opt out of public display. Opted-out records are removed only from SAM public search and stay visible to federal users with FOUO access. Fix: search cage.dla.mil, or ask the company for a screenshot of its SAM record.
  • Copying the first hit. Similar names are common. Always match the address and UEI.

CAGE Code Lookup on SAM.gov: What You Can and Can't See

SAM.gov shows public CAGE codes for registered entities for free. It doesn't let you request a new CAGE code. New codes come from your own SAM registration or from DLA's CAGE system.

Without logging in, you can seeYou can't see or do
Legal business name, physical address, registration statusRecords of entities that opted out of public display
UEI and CAGE/NCAGE codePoints of contact and other FOUO data (federal users only)
Expiration date of the SAM registrationRequest or edit a CAGE code for another company
Exclusions (search the Exclusions domain)CAGE codes for companies that never registered in SAM

Enabling public search puts a registrant's record status, legal business name, and physical address in front of non-federal viewers. Opting out may reduce business opportunities, because prime contractors can't find subcontractors who opted out. If you're a small business hoping to be found for teaming, leave public display on.

Finding your own CAGE code

  1. Sign in to SAM.gov.
  2. Open Workspace and select your entity under Entity Management.
  3. Read the CAGE code in the entity's core data.

If registration is still processing, check SAM.gov's Status Tracker. It shows where your registration stands, and when SAM can't validate your entity you can open a Federal Service Desk ticket from that page.

Pitfalls

  • Treating SAM as the master record. SAM displays the CAGE code, but the CAGE record itself is DLA's. If the address in your CAGE record looks wrong, correct it through your SAM registration update (for SAM registrants), which feeds DLA. Don't fix it in only one place.
  • Assuming "Active" means eligible. An active registration doesn't mean the company isn't excluded. Run an Exclusions search in the same tool before you sign a teaming agreement.

CAGE Code Lookup via DLA: When You Need the Official Source

DLA Logistics Information Service runs the CAGE system of record. Use cage.dla.mil when SAM.gov has no record, when the SAM record looks outdated, or when you need to request or update a CAGE code directly. DLA describes CAGE Public as including CAGE Search and Inquiry (CSI) and CAGE Request, a single place to search codes, find forms, request a new code or update an existing one.

When DLA beats SAM.gov

  • The company has a CAGE code but never registered in SAM. Many manufacturers in the federal parts catalog fall into this group.
  • The company opted out of SAM public display.
  • You need the CAGE record's status, such as active, obsolete or replaced, rather than the SAM registration status.
  • You're a U.S. entity that needs a code without registering in SAM (FAR 52.204-16).

Steps to search cage.dla.mil

  1. Open cage.dla.mil in Chrome, Edge or Firefox. The site says it requires cookies and supports those three browsers.
  2. Accept the usage agreement.
  3. Choose search & inquiry.
  4. Enter a CAGE code or company name. Use the advanced search options to narrow by location when a name returns many matches.
  5. Open the record and read the status and address before relying on the code.

Steps to request a CAGE code directly (non-SAM U.S. entities)

  1. On cage.dla.mil, choose request | update.
  2. Search first to confirm your entity doesn't already have a code. A duplicate request creates cleanup work later.
  3. Complete the request form with your legal name and physical location exactly as they appear on your formation documents.
  4. Keep the confirmation details. Questions go to the DLA Customer Interaction Center at 1-877-352-2255 (number listed on cage.dla.mil).

Official numbers to know (as of October 2026)

  • A CAGE code is five characters (DLA CAGE program description).
  • An entity with a CAGE code must renew it every five years. For SAM registrants, the required annual SAM renewal keeps the CAGE record updated.
  • CAGE program phone: toll-free 1-877-352-2255, commercial 1-269-961-7766 (PIEE vendor guide).

Pitfall

If you register in SAM later, don't request a second code. Tell SAM about your existing CAGE code during registration so DLA links the records.

Free CAGE Code Lookup Tools: Are They Reliable?

Free third-party CAGE lookup sites exist, but only SAM.gov and DLA are authoritative and current. Third-party sites copy public data and can fall behind official updates. Many are built on DLA's public extracts. PUB LOG, for example, is updated monthly and posted on the first business day of each month, so any site built on it can be weeks behind.

SourceAuthoritative?FreshnessLogin neededBest forNot for
SAM.gov Entity InformationYes, for SAM registrationsLiveNoQuick name/UEI checks, exclusionsOpted-out or never-registered firms
cage.dla.mil (CSI)Yes, system of recordLiveNo (usage agreement)Any CAGE, including non-SAM firmsBulk exports
PUB LOG / PUB LOG FLIS SearchYes, DLA public dataMonthlyNoPart number → CAGESame-day changes
Third-party lookup sitesNoVaries; often undatedSometimesConvenience, bulk lists, cross-linksAnything you'll put in a proposal or contract

Pitfalls and fixes

  • The site shows no "last updated" date. Treat it as a lead, not proof. Confirm the code on SAM.gov or cage.dla.mil before it goes into a proposal.
  • Upsell pages that look official. Some sites offer to "get your CAGE code" for a fee. FAR 52.204-16 describes free routes through SAM.gov and cage.dla.mil. SAM registration is free, and NCAGE codes are normally issued without charge by national bureaus.
  • Stale ownership data. After a merger, the old code may be replaced. Check the CAGE status on DLA's record.

How to Look Up a CAGE Code by Part Number

To find a CAGE code from a part number, search the Federal Logistics Information System (FLIS) through DLA's free PUB LOG FLIS Search. SAM.gov can't search parts. FLIS links each manufacturer part number to the CAGE code of the company that makes it or controls the design.

The full WebFLIS tool is restricted. DLA now limits it to DLA, the Military Services and U.S. government-sponsored contractors. Public users go through the FOIA reading room's PUB LOG FLIS Search (DLA FLIS Data Electronic Reading Room). PUB LOG is DLA's public product for NSN data, FSC data and CAGE codes, offered as free downloads.

Steps

  1. Open the FLIS Data Electronic Reading Room and launch PUB LOG FLIS Search.
  2. Choose a part number search. Partial part numbers are supported, which helps when the drawing number has suffixes.
  3. Enter the part number as printed, without spaces you aren't sure of.
  4. In the results, each part number row shows the CAGE code attached to that reference along with the NSN.
  5. Copy the CAGE code and look it up on cage.dla.mil to get the company name, address and status.

Example

If a solicitation lists "NSN 5305-XX-XXX-XXXX, P/N ABC123, CAGE 1XXXX" as an approved source (placeholder values), you can do two things. Search the NSN to see every part number and CAGE code cataloged against it. Search the CAGE code to see who the approved manufacturer is. That tells you whether you're quoting as the manufacturer, as an authorized distributor, or as an alternate source needing approval. Our guide RFQ vs RFP: 5 FAR Clues and What to Submit covers how parts RFQs differ from full proposals.

Pitfalls

  • One part number, many CAGE codes. Common part numbers repeat across manufacturers. Always pair the part number with the expected CAGE code.
  • Monthly data. A part added to the catalog last week may not appear yet. For anything urgent, ask the contracting officer.
  • Distributor codes. A distributor's CAGE code identifies the distributor, not the manufacturer. If the solicitation requires the original manufacturer's code, quote that one.

CAGE Code Lookup Tools Compared: SAM.gov vs. DLA vs. Third-Party

SAM.gov is best for quick name checks on registered contractors. DLA is the system of record for all CAGE data, including firms that never touched SAM. Third-party tools add convenience features such as bulk lists, but they aren't authoritative. Match the tool to the job:

TaskBest toolWhyLimitation
Name search for a likely bidderSAM.gov Entity InformationShows CAGE, UEI, status and exclusions togetherMisses opted-out entities
Address or location checkcage.dla.mil, then SAM.gov recordDLA records are location-specificName or code usually needed to start
Part number → manufacturerPUB LOG FLIS SearchOnly free public source tied to the catalogUpdated monthly
Teaming due diligenceSAM.gov + Exclusions + DLAConfirms the code, active registration and no exclusionSize status needs separate checks
Bulk list of hundreds of codesSAM.gov Entity Management API or a third-party toolAPI gives structured, official public dataOpted-out records hidden from public API keys
Foreign partnerNSPA NCAGE toolNCAGE codes are issued by national bureausProcess runs through another country's office

A teaming due-diligence checklist (CAGE part)

Before signing a teaming agreement:

  1. Confirm the partner's CAGE code and UEI match the facility that will do the work.
  2. Confirm the SAM registration is Active and won't expire during the proposal window.
  3. Run an Exclusions search on the name, UEI and CAGE code.
  4. If FAR 52.204-17 applies, collect CAGE codes for the immediate and highest-level owners.
  5. Then check size under the solicitation's NAICS code using our SBA Size Standards by NAICS guide. On set-asides, also check how much work each partner performs with our Small Business Set Aside 51 Rule checklist.

How to Look Up a CAGE Code by Address

SAM.gov's public search has no standard address filter. In practice, search by company name first and check the address on the entity record, or use the location fields in DLA's CAGE search. This matters because a CAGE code identifies an entity at a specific location. The address is part of what the code means.

Steps

  1. Search SAM.gov Entity Information by name and use any location filters shown (state, ZIP) to narrow the list.
  2. Open each candidate and compare the physical address line by line, including suite numbers.
  3. If no SAM record matches, search cage.dla.mil by name and narrow by location in the advanced search.
  4. If you have an address but truly no name, use a name from the property's signage, a business license or a state business registry. Then repeat steps 1–3.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Mailing address vs. physical address. CAGE records are tied to the physical location. A P.O. box or registered-agent address won't match.
  • The company moved. A move can mean an updated CAGE record or a new code. If the address you hold is old, the CAGE code you hold may be too. Ask the company to confirm.
  • Shared buildings. Coworking addresses can host dozens of registrants. Match name, address and UEI together.

CAGE Code Lookup Outside the U.S.: Does Australia (or Other Allies) Use CAGE Codes?

Yes. Outside the U.S., the same five-character identifier is called an NCAGE code. Australian and other foreign suppliers get one through their national codification bureau, via NSPA, not from DLA. CAGE codes are used across the NATO Codification System, where they're sometimes called NCAGE codes. Foreign offerors are directed to their country's NATO codification bureau or NSPA under FAR 52.204-16.

A foreign entity must obtain an NCAGE code before it can complete SAM.gov registration. That reverses the U.S. order, where SAM triggers the CAGE code.

Steps for a foreign company (Australia as the example)

  1. Go to the NSPA NATO Codification Tools ePortal at eportal.nspa.nato.int/ac135public and select CAGE/NCAGE Code Request (U.S. Embassy instructions for NSPA NCAGE).
  2. Search for your entity first. If it's not found, click Request New, fill in all required fields and submit.
  3. Watch for the validation email sent to the point of contact on the request. Click the embedded link to confirm, or the request won't move forward.
  4. NSPA routes the request to your country's bureau. In Australia, NCAGE matters are handled by the National Codification Bureau within the Department of Defence (vendor cell contact listed in the embassy instructions: NCB.VendorCellOps@defence.gov.au).
  5. Once the NCAGE code is issued, register in SAM.gov and enter the NCAGE code where SAM asks for it.

Pitfalls

  • Legal name mismatch. The name on the NCAGE record must match the name you'll use in SAM. Small differences such as "Pty Ltd" vs. "Pty. Limited" can stall SAM validation.
  • Ignoring the confirmation email. It goes to the point of contact you named. Use a monitored address.
  • Looking up an Australian partner on SAM.gov only. If they haven't registered in SAM, search the NSPA tool or cage.dla.mil instead. Both cover NCAGE records.

Next steps

You can finish most of this today without paying anyone.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Search your own company on SAM.gov Entity Information. Confirm your CAGE code, address and registration expiry, and note the date your next renewal is due.
  2. For any teaming partner you plan to name in a proposal, run the five-item due-diligence checklist above and save the SAM record and Exclusions results with the date.
  3. If you sell parts, run your top five part numbers through PUB LOG FLIS Search to see which CAGE codes the government associates with them.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) give no-cost help with SAM registration, certifications and bid reviews. Find yours at apexaccelerators.us (no fee as of October 2026; check the official page). Good for first-time bidders who want a person to walk through SAM. Not ideal if you need same-day turnaround, since appointments depend on local staffing.
  • DLA Customer Interaction Center, 1-877-352-2255 (cage.dla.mil), handles CAGE record questions for free. It's for record problems, not for bid strategy.
  • Paid registration services charge for steps the government provides free. They may suit a firm that wants to hand off all the paperwork, but they can't speed up DLA or IRS validation. Check pricing on the provider's own page before you agree to anything.

Related guides on Set-Aside Brief:

  • Sources Sought Notice: 5-Step Response Template (2026)

FAQ

How do I do a CAGE code lookup on SAM.gov?

Open sam.gov, click Search, choose the Entity Information domain and enter the company's legal name or UEI. The CAGE/NCAGE code appears on the entity record without a login. If nothing appears, the company may have opted out of public display or never registered. In that case, try cage.dla.mil.

How do I do a CAGE code lookup on DLA's site?

Go to cage.dla.mil, accept the usage agreement and choose search & inquiry. You can search by CAGE code or company name. DLA's records include entities that never registered in SAM. For problems with a record, call the DLA Customer Interaction Center at 1-877-352-2255.

Can I do a CAGE code lookup by part number?

Yes. Use DLA's public PUB LOG FLIS Search in the FLIS Data Electronic Reading Room, which supports full and partial part number searches. The data updates monthly, so very recent catalog changes may not show yet. The full WebFLIS tool is limited to government users and sponsored contractors.

Do Australian companies have CAGE codes?

Yes. Australian companies receive NCAGE codes, the NATO-system version of the same identifier. They request them through the NSPA ePortal, and Australia's National Codification Bureau at the Department of Defence handles the request. An Australian firm needs the NCAGE code before it can complete SAM.gov registration.

Do I need to request a CAGE code separately after registering in SAM.gov?

No. For U.S. entities, DLA's CAGE Branch assigns the code as part of SAM registration under FAR 52.204-16. Request one directly at cage.dla.mil only if you're a U.S. entity that doesn't otherwise register in SAM.

item.title: Subcontracting Government Contracts: 6 Steps to Get Started
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Subcontracting government contracts in 2026: find primes with FAR 52.219-9 plans, use SBA SubNet and Small Business Search, and avoid common sub mistakes.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To start subcontracting on government contracts, register in SAM.gov, finish your SBA Small Business Search profile, and go after large prime contractors whose contracts carry a FAR 52.219-9 small business subcontracting plan. Those plans require primes to set dollar goals for small, veteran-owned, service-disabled veteran-owned, HUBZone, small disadvantaged and women-owned subcontractors, and to report how they did against them. You get picked when you fill a gap in that plan: the right NAICS code, the right status, and a pitch that a prime's small business liaison can approve fast. SBA's SubNet board, its prime contractor directory and agency matchmaking events are where those primes are looking (as of October 2026).

Which option is right for you?

Your best first move depends on whether you are registered yet, how much time you have each week and how much you can spend.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, no SAM.gov registration yetGet your UEI and an active registration. Primes and SBA's search tool only see registered firmsSAM.gov and our SAM.gov registration guide
Registered, want leads this weekSBA SubNet listings, filtered by your state and keywords. These are live requests from primes with closing datesSBA SubNet listings
Daily business development workThe SBA prime contractor directory, sorted by your NAICS code and state, so you can build a target listDirectory of prime contractors with subcontracting plans
Want primes to find youA complete Small Business Search profile with keywords, NAICS codes and certificationsSBA Small Business Search
Tight budget, need guidanceFree or nominal-cost counseling from an APEX AcceleratorMaryland APEX example or your state's center
Mostly state work (for example, Missouri)State bid board plus state MBE/WBE certification, not federal toolsMissouriBUYS and Missouri OEO certification

If you only do one thing today, start with the row that matches where you are now. Skipping steps is how you end up with a polished pitch nobody can find in a search.

How to Subcontract Government Contracts

To subcontract government contracts, register in SAM.gov, confirm your size under your NAICS code, then pitch primes whose contracts include FAR 52.219-9 subcontracting plans. Here are the six steps in order.

Step 1: Get an active SAM.gov registration

Primes can accept your size and status straight from SAM.gov. FAR 19.703 says a prime "may accept a subcontractor's written representations of its size and socioeconomic status" or rely on what you've entered in SAM. SBA's Small Business Search, which replaced the old Dynamic Small Business Search on July 9, 2025, only lists businesses with an active SAM registration (FedBiz Access). Our SAM.gov registration guide walks through each screen from UEI to "Active."

Step 2: Confirm your size under each NAICS code you list

Small business status is tied to a NAICS code. A firm can be small under one code and large under another. Look up each code you plan to list in SBA size standards by NAICS before you claim "small" on a prime's supplier form.

Step 3: Decide which statuses you can honestly claim

Under FAR 19.703, small business, SDB, WOSB, VOSB and SDVOSB status for subcontract goal credit can rest on your own written representation, as long as it is "current, accurate, and complete as of the date of the offer." HUBZone status is handled separately: FAR 19.703 directs that protests of a subcontractor's HUBZone status be filed under 13 CFR 126.801. Being certified still helps. For example, a WOSB-certified firm gives the prime's compliance team one less thing to check.

Step 4: Build a target list of primes that must subcontract

A subcontracting plan is required when a contract awarded to a large business is expected to exceed $900,000, or $2,000,000 for construction. Small businesses, personal services contracts and contracts performed entirely outside the U.S. are exempt (FAR 19.702, as of October 2026). These amounts went up from $750,000 and $1.5 million on October 1, 2025, as part of the FAR inflation adjustment (SmallGovCon).

SBA's Directory of Federal Government Prime Contractors with Subcontracting Plans is an Excel file. Its columns include vendor name and location, contracting agency, PSC, NAICS code, state of performance, contract number (PIID), performance dates and total contract value. The data comes from FPDS, and the page was last updated March 4, 2025, so check any contract you find against current award data.

Step 5: Match your pitch to the prime's plan

Every plan has to list the principal types of supplies and services the prime expects to subcontract. It also has to name an employee who will administer the program (FAR 19.704). That administrator, usually called the small business liaison officer, is your first contact. Lead with a one-page capability statement that shows your NAICS codes, statuses and relevant past work.

Step 6: Respond to live requests and register on primes' supplier portals

Answer SubNet postings and teaming requests before they close. Most large primes also run their own supplier registration portals, so register on the ones that match your list.

How to Find Subcontractors for Government Contracts

Primes find subcontractors through SBA SubNet, SBA's Small Business Search, agency small business offices and matchmaking events. Knowing how they search tells you how to get found.

FAR 52.219-9(e) expects primes to make an outreach effort, including using SAM, veterans service organizations and small business trade associations to find sources, and to give small firms enough time to prepare bids. FAR 19.705-7 lists "insufficient market research to identify small business sources" as one sign that a prime failed to make a good faith effort. That gives primes a documented reason to search.

Tool a prime usesWhat it searchesWhat you control
SBA Small Business SearchBusiness name, NAICS codes, keywords and capabilities, location, certificationsYour SAM data and the profile sections you edit after claiming your listing
SBA SubNetPrimes post a need; small firms respondSpeed and quality of your response
Agency directories (SBA names Defense, DOT, GSA and USDA resources)Agency-specific prime listsWhich agencies you target (SBA)
GSA small business resourcesGSA prime and subcontracting informationWhich schedules and categories you follow

For example, say a prime needs a HUBZone electrical subcontractor in Ohio. It might search Small Business Search for NAICS 238210 with the HUBZone filter and the state set to Ohio. If your keywords say "electrical" but leave out "low-voltage" or "fire alarm," a narrower keyword search can miss you. Fill the capabilities narrative with the specific words a buyer would type.

Limitation: Small Business Search only reflects what's in SAM.gov plus SBA certification data. It doesn't show past performance quality, so a profile alone rarely wins work. It is not a good fit for firms that aren't registered yet, because they won't appear at all.

Subcontracting Government Contracts: Reddit Discussions and What's Actually True

Forum threads tend to say subcontracting is easier than it is and that primes "owe" small businesses work. In reality, primes pick their subs, goals are not per-contract quotas, and payment disputes are real.

Here are claims you'll often see in discussion threads, checked against the regulations.

"The prime has to give me work because of its plan." Not quite. FAR 19.704 sets goals as "a percentage of total subcontract dollars," across all of the prime's subcontracting, not for any one vendor. The prime chooses which small businesses get those dollars. The one firm commitment tied to specific firms is a good faith effort to use the small businesses it named in its proposal (FAR 52.219-9). If you were named in a proposal and then dropped, that matters. If you were never named, the prime owes you nothing.

"Plans are meaningless; nobody enforces them." That's overstated. Failing to comply in good faith with an approved plan is "a material breach of the contract" (FAR 52.219-9). The government can also assess liquidated damages equal to "the actual dollar amount by which the contractor failed to achieve each subcontracting goal" (FAR 19.705-7). How hard any agency enforces this varies, but the tools exist.

"Primes pay subs whenever they want." Partly true in practice. The plan, though, requires primes to pay small business subs "on time and in accordance with the terms and conditions." They must also notify the contracting officer of reduced or untimely payments, which the clause defines as more than 90 days past due (FAR 52.219-9). Primes also can't stop you from discussing payment problems with the contracting officer.

"Teaming agreements guarantee work." Not true. A teaming agreement signed before award usually promises a subcontract only if the prime wins and the parties agree on terms. Read the exit clauses before you sign.

Subcontracting Federal Contracts: Key Rules You Need to Know

Contracts above the plan threshold that have subcontracting possibilities require the prime to submit a FAR 52.219-9 plan with separate percentage goals. The clause then flows down to subcontractors that receive large subcontracts.

RuleWhat it saysNumber (as of Oct 2026)Source
Plan thresholdLarge primes need a plan above this value$900,000; $2,000,000 constructionFAR 19.702
Goal categoriesSeparate goals for SB, VOSB, SDVOSB, HUBZone, SDB, WOSB6 categoriesFAR 52.219-9
Goal basisPercent of total subcontract dollarsNot a percent of the contract unless the CO asksFAR 19.704
ISR reportingIndividual Subcontract Report, twice a yearPeriods ending Mar 31 and Sep 30; due 30 days laterFAR 52.219-9
SSR reportingSummary Subcontract ReportAnnually by Oct 30FAR 52.219-9
Reporting systemeSRS.gov retired; reports moved into SAM.govFeb 20, 2026SAM.gov announcement
Flow-downSubs getting subcontracts over the FAR 19.702 threshold that offer further subcontracting must adopt their own planSame $900,000 / $2MFAR 52.219-9(d)(9)
Losing bidder noticeFor competitive subcontracts over the simplified acquisition threshold where a small business preference applied, the prime tells unsuccessful small offerors who wonSAT is $350,000FAR 52.219-9; SmallGovCon

FAR 52.219-9 (January 2025 version) still names esrs.gov in its text, while SAM.gov now hosts reporting at sam.gov/esrs. Industry write-ups describe the move as a system change with the same deadlines, and say access is now tied to UEI and PIID (iQuasar).

The flow-down rule is the one most first-time subs miss. If you, as a small business, win a $1.2 million non-construction subcontract from a large prime and it offers further subcontracting, you aren't asked for a plan, because small businesses are exempt under FAR 19.702. A large-business sub in the same position would have to adopt one. Either way, read the clause list attached to your purchase order. Primes routinely flow down dozens of FAR and DFARS clauses, and you're bound by each one you accept.

Pitfall: Treating the plan as the prime's paperwork and none of your business. If the prime reports you as a WOSB in SAM.gov and you aren't, the misrepresentation is yours. FAR 19.703 protects primes that rely on representations in good faith, which leaves the risk with you.

Outsourcing Government Contracts: Is It the Same as Subcontracting?

No. "Outsourcing" is everyday business language, while federal "subcontracting" is a legal relationship governed by flow-down clauses, the limitations on subcontracting and plan reporting.

Informal "outsourcing"Federal subcontracting
DefinitionAny work sent outside the firmA contract under a prime contract, subject to the prime's clauses
Rules that applyYour commercial contractFlow-downs plus, on set-asides, FAR 52.219-14
ReportingNoneCounted in the prime's ISR/SSR in SAM.gov when a plan applies
Risk if mislabeledLowA small prime can break the limits on subcontracting

The term matters most when you're the small prime on a set-aside. Under FAR 52.219-14 (October 2022), you can't pay non-similarly situated subcontractors more than these shares of what the government pays you:

  • Services: 50% of the amount paid for contract performance
  • Supplies (not as a nonmanufacturer): 50%, excluding the cost of materials
  • General construction: 85%, excluding materials
  • Special trade construction: 75%, excluding materials

Work done by a similarly situated subcontractor, meaning one with the same small business status as the prime, counts toward the prime's own share. That gives you a pitch. If you're a small business subbing to a small business prime on a small business set-aside, your work doesn't eat into the prime's 50%. A large-business sub's work does. Our 51 rule checklist covers the math.

Pitfall: Calling a 1099 contractor or a staffing vendor "outsourced help" and leaving them out of your subcontracting count. If they perform contract work, their dollars probably count toward the limit. Track them on the same spreadsheet as your other subs.

Missouri Government Contracts: State and Local Subcontracting Opportunities

Missouri state contracting is separate from federal SAM.gov and SubNet. Use MissouriBUYS for state bids and Missouri's Office of Equal Opportunity (OEO) for MBE/WBE/SDVE certification.

People often assume one registration covers both. It doesn't. Here's how to get set up for Missouri state work:

  1. Register as a supplier in MissouriBUYS. The state's purchasing page tells suppliers to "register now in the new MissouriBUYS, powered by MOVERS." The system handles vendor self-registration, solicitations, the bid board and online bidding (Missouri Office of Administration).
  2. If you qualify, apply for state certification. OEO runs the MBE, WBE, SDVE and HDVE programs. MBE/WBE requires that "at least 51 percent of the business must be owned by a minority and/or a woman," who must hold the top position and control the business (OEO). There's no application fee, and the standard process for Missouri-based businesses takes about 60 to 90 days (OEO FAQs, as of October 2026). Note that certification sits with OEO, not the economic development office some guides point to.
  3. Get listed in the directory primes use. Certified firms appear in the Directory of Certified M/WBE Vendors. OEO says "both contractors and state agencies use this site as a resource in soliciting certified minority and/or female participation." State primes report their certified sub participation on the "MBE/WBE, Blind/Sheltered Workshop, and SDVE Participation Report" form (Missouri OA).
  4. Check certified-only notices. OEO says that beyond the MissouriBUYS bid board, "additional procurement opportunities are shared with certified MBE, WBE, HDVE, and SDVE vendors" (OEO).

Missouri state certification doesn't make you a federal WOSB or 8(a) firm, and federal certification doesn't automatically carry over to the state list. For federal work in Missouri, you still need SAM.gov and the federal tools above. The Missouri APEX Accelerator, which the state's purchasing page links to, helps with both.

How to Read and Respond to a Prime's SBA SubNet Listing

A SubNet listing names the prime, the work, the NAICS codes, where it will be performed and the closing date. Respond to the listed contact before closing with a matched capability statement, relevant past performance and your statuses.

As of October 2026, SubNet listings are on SBA's legacy site. You can filter by state and keyword and sort by clicking column headers (SBA SubNet). SBA's newer contracting guide says small firms can view postings by contacting subcontracting@sba.gov (SBA). If the board doesn't load, use that address. Primes don't post directly. They email subcontracting@sba.gov to get a listing up, and posts "meant only to promote your small business will be removed." So don't post an ad for your own firm.

Each listing includes the business name, project description, closing date, performance start date, place of performance (state), NAICS code(s) and a point of contact with email and phone.

How to respond:

  1. Filter by your state, then by keyword (for example, "janitorial" or "HVAC"). Sort by closing date so the soonest deadlines are at the top.
  2. Check the NAICS code against your SAM registration. If the listing says 561720 and you're registered only under 561210, add the code in SAM.gov first, provided you actually do that work.
  3. Check the place of performance and start date against your capacity. A start date six weeks out means the prime needs someone who is ready now.
  4. Email the listed contact. Use a subject line with the listing title and your status, for example: "Linen services, Oregon – WOSB, NAICS 812332."
  5. Attach a one-page capability statement. Put your UEI and CAGE code (see our CAGE code guide), statuses, two or three similar jobs with contract numbers or customer names you're allowed to share, and a direct contact.
  6. Answer every question in the posting. If it asks for bonding, insurance limits or a price range, give it. An incomplete reply is easy to skip.
  7. Follow up once before the closing date. Then get on the prime's supplier portal whatever the outcome, so you're in their system for the next need.

For example, a listing for water system construction in Montana with a near-term closing date is a poor fit for a Florida firm with no Montana license. Skip it and spend the time on listings where your NAICS code, state and timing all line up.

Limitation: SubNet carries a small number of postings compared with all subcontracting activity. Many primes fill needs through their own portals without ever posting. Treat SubNet as one lead source, next to the prime directory.

Common Pitfalls First-Time Subcontractors Face on Federal Work

New subs usually stumble on four things: an incomplete registration, statuses they can't support, flow-down terms nobody read, and loose payment terms. Each one can cost you the award or your margin.

PitfallWhat happensFix
SAM.gov registration lapsed or never finishedYou drop out of Small Business Search, and the prime can't verify your status in SAMRenew before expiration; see the registration guide
Claiming a status you don't holdMisrepresentation risk falls on you, since FAR 19.703 shields primes acting in good faithRepresent only what's true as of the offer date; get certified where it helps
Signing the PO without reading the flow-downsYou're bound by clauses on cybersecurity, labor or reporting you can't meetAsk for the clause list before pricing; price compliance costs in
Vague payment termsCash crunch on 60–90 day cyclesWrite net terms and invoice requirements into the subcontract. If you're over 90 days past due, know the prime must report it and can't stop you from talking to the CO (FAR 52.219-9)
Wrong NAICS code on your pitchThe prime's search or goal coding doesn't matchLine up SAM, Small Business Search and capability statement codes
Pitching the wrong peopleEmails to generic sales inboxes go nowhereContact the plan administrator or small business liaison officer named under FAR 19.704

One more to watch: getting named in a prime's proposal as a small business teaming partner and then hearing nothing after award. The prime must make a good faith effort to use the small businesses it named in its proposal (FAR 52.219-9). If you're dropped without explanation, you can raise it with the contracting officer. SBA's Commercial Market Representatives also help with post-award plan compliance (SBA).

Next steps

Pick one or two of these and finish them today.

DIY actions for today:

  1. Open SAM.gov and check that your registration is "Active." Note the expiration date, and confirm the NAICS codes match the work you want to sub on.
  2. Download SBA's prime contractor directory. Filter by your NAICS code and state, and keep 10 primes with performance dates still running.
  3. Open the SubNet listings, filter by your state, and answer one posting that matches your NAICS code before it closes.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: APEX Accelerators, formerly PTACs, offer one-on-one counseling on registration, market research and subcontracting. Services are free or offered at a nominal cost (as of October 2026; check the official page), and the program is administered through the Department of Defense (Washington APEX; Maryland APEX). APEX suits owners who want guidance and will do the work themselves. It's a poor fit if you want someone to write and submit responses for you: counselors advise but don't run your business development, and appointment availability varies by center. Private proposal consultants will do that hands-on work. Their fees vary widely and aren't standardized, so get a written scope and price before you sign.

Related guides on this site:

  • How to Bid on Government Contracts: 7 Steps, 2026 Costs, for when you're ready to go after prime work too

FAQ

What is a FAR 52.219-9 subcontracting plan?

It's the contract clause that makes a large prime set separate goals for subcontracting to small, VOSB, SDVOSB, HUBZone, SDB and WOSB firms. The prime also has to name a program administrator and report results twice a year (ISR) and once a year (SSR). It applies to contracts above $900,000, or $2 million for construction, as of October 2026 (FAR 19.702). Not complying in good faith counts as a material breach.

How do I register as a subcontractor on SBA SubNet?

Small businesses don't register on SubNet. You browse the listings and contact the prime named in each one. The board is on SBA's legacy site with state and keyword filters, and SBA also says you can ask for postings through subcontracting@sba.gov (SBA). To be found by primes, make sure you show up in Small Business Search, which requires an active SAM registration.

Do I need a small business certification to subcontract on federal contracts?

Usually not. Under FAR 19.703, primes may accept your written representation, or your SAM.gov representation, of small business, SDB, WOSB, VOSB or SDVOSB status. HUBZone status is handled separately, with protests of a subcontractor's HUBZone status filed under 13 CFR 126.801. Certification can still make a prime more comfortable picking you, and you need it to compete for certain set-aside prime contracts.

What's the difference between a subcontracting plan goal and a set-aside?

A set-aside limits who can bid on the prime contract itself, for example only small businesses. A subcontracting plan goal is a target percentage of a large prime's subcontract dollars that should go to small firms (FAR 19.704). Set-asides decide who can win the prime contract. Plan goals affect who gets the subcontracts underneath it.

Where do I find Missouri state government subcontracting opportunities?

Register on MissouriBUYS for state bids. If you qualify, get MBE, WBE or SDVE certification from Missouri's Office of Equal Opportunity. There's no application fee, and it takes about 60 to 90 days for Missouri-based firms (OEO FAQs). Certified firms are listed in the state directory that primes use to find participation partners.

item.title: NAICS Code for Construction: 2026 Size Table and Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: The NAICS code for construction depends on your trade. Compare 236, 237 and 238 codes, SBA size limits and steps to pick the code that keeps you eligible.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

No single NAICS code covers all of construction. Construction is NAICS Sector 23, and inside it you choose a 6-digit code from three subsectors: 236 for building construction (general contractors and homebuilders), 237 for heavy and civil engineering, and 238 for specialty trades. Use the code that brings in the largest share of your receipts. The code you pick also sets your SBA size standard. Under the current table, most 236 and 237 codes allow $45 million in average annual receipts and most 238 trade codes allow $19 million (13 CFR 121.201, as of October 2026).

Which option is right for you?

Find your situation in the table, then open the page listed for it before you change anything in SAM.gov.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time bidder, one trade (for example, only roofing)The single 238xxx code for that trade, set as your primaryCensus NAICS search
General contractor running commercial or institutional jobs236220 as primary, plus the 238 codes you self-perform as secondary codesSBA size standards table
Homebuilder or remodeler236115, 236116, 236117 or 236118, matched to how your revenue actually comes in13 CFR 121.201
Roads, utilities, site and civil workThe matching 237xxx code. If you dredge, check the dredging rule13 CFR 121.201
Consultant, CM-agent or estimator with no construction risk541330, 541611 or 541990, not a Sector 23 codeCensus NAICS search
Small budget, want free help checking your choiceA free APEX Accelerator counseling sessionAPEX Accelerators

The reasons, one line each:

  • Beginner: Start with one accurate primary code. Listing twenty codes does not make you more eligible, and you have to defend each one if your size is ever protested.
  • Daily bidding work: Each solicitation names its own NAICS code, so you need every code you might bid under in SAM.gov, not only the primary.
  • Budget: Census lookups, the SBA table and APEX counseling are free. Paid help is only worth considering if your revenue sits close to a size threshold.

What Is the NAICS Code for Construction? (Overview + How Sector 23 Is Organized)

The NAICS code for construction is Sector 23, which splits into three 3-digit subsectors and dozens of 6-digit industry codes. You register and bid under the 6-digit codes. "23" alone is never what goes on a SAM.gov profile or a solicitation.

Each subsector covers a different kind of work:

SubsectorWhat it coversExample 6-digit codesTypical SBA size standard
236 Construction of BuildingsFirms responsible for whole buildings: GCs, homebuilders, remodelers236115, 236116, 236117, 236118, 236210, 236220$45.0M
237 Heavy and Civil Engineering ConstructionUtilities, roads, bridges, land subdivision, other civil work237110, 237120, 237130, 237210, 237310, 237990$45.0M (237210: $34.0M; 237990 dredging: $37.0M)
238 Specialty Trade ContractorsOne trade, usually as a subcontractor: concrete, roofing, electrical, HVAC, drywall, flooring238110–238990$19.0M (238290: $22.0M)

All size figures come from 13 CFR 121.201 (as of October 2026) and match the SBA table that took effect March 17, 2023 (SBA).

The line between 236 and 238 is responsibility. Census places firms that perform specialized work on commercial and institutional buildings, "generally on a subcontract basis," in Subsector 238 rather than 236220 (NAICS 236220 description). A firm that takes responsibility for the whole building belongs in 236. A firm that installs one system in someone else's building belongs in 238.

Pitfall: Some third-party lists print wrong size figures. For example, at least one 2026 guide lists 236118 at $22.0M. The regulation sets $45.0M for 236118, and $22.0M is actually the figure for 238290 (13 CFR 121.201). Before you rely on any number, check it against the regulation or the SBA table.

How to Choose the Right NAICS Code When Your Trade Spans Multiple Codes

Pick the code that brings in the largest share of your receipts. Don't pick the one that sounds most impressive, because the code decides which size standard applies to you. SBA looks at "the distribution of receipts, employees and costs of doing business among the different industries" for your most recently completed fiscal year to decide your primary industry (13 CFR 121.107).

Steps to pick your primary code

  1. Pull last fiscal year's revenue by job type. Use your job-costing or accounting reports. Group every job into what you actually did: whole-building responsibility, civil/site work, or a single trade.
  2. Look up each group's code. Open the Census NAICS search, choose the 2022 NAICS edition, and type a plain keyword such as "drywall" or "highway." Read the full definition and the cross-references, not only the title.
  3. Rank the groups by receipts. The biggest group is your primary-code candidate. If two groups are close, compare employee hours and costs too, since SBA weighs those as well (13 CFR 121.107).
  4. Check each code's size standard. Find each code in the SBA table. Compare it with your average annual receipts, which for a firm 5+ years old is total receipts over the last 5 completed fiscal years divided by 5 (13 CFR 121.104). Count affiliates' receipts too.
  5. Enter the codes in SAM.gov. Log in, open your entity, choose Update Entity Registration, go to the Goods and Services section, add each 6-digit NAICS code, and mark one as primary (SmallGovCon). Our SAM.gov registration guide walks through the rest of the record.
  6. Add secondary codes only for work you can actually perform. Each code you list is a claim you may have to back up.

Worked example

This example is for illustration only. A firm averages $24M a year. Last year's revenue was 60% commercial building jobs where it was the prime, 30% self-performed electrical subcontracts, and 10% small residential remodels.

  • Primary: 236220, which has a $45.0M standard. The firm is small under it.
  • Secondary: 238210 Electrical Contractors, which has a $19.0M standard. The firm is not small under it, because size is measured on the whole firm's receipts, not just the electrical slice.
  • Secondary: 236118, which has a $45.0M standard. The firm is small under it.

So the firm can compete for small business set-asides coded 236220 or 236118. It cannot compete for an electrical set-aside coded 238210, even though electrical is real work it performs. Picking codes is a two-way decision: the code has to match the work, and your size has to fit under it.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Mistake: Making 238xxx your primary because you started out as a trade sub, even though most revenue now comes from GC work. Fix: Recheck your revenue mix every year when you renew your SAM registration.
  • Mistake: Assuming the primary code decides every bid. Fix: For a specific contract, the contracting officer names the governing code (see the last main section below).
  • Mistake: Forgetting affiliates. Fix: Add the receipts of any company under common control before you compare against the standard.

What Is the NAICS Code for a Construction Company (General Contractor)?

For a construction company that takes responsibility for whole buildings, the code is usually 236220 (commercial and institutional) or one of 236115–236118 (residential). Industrial plants use 236210. Pick based on what you build, not on the name of your company.

CodeTitleUse it when you…Size standard
236115New Single-Family Housing Construction (except For-Sale Builders)Build single-family homes for owners on their land$45.0M
236116New Multifamily Housing Construction (except For-Sale Builders)Build apartments or condos as a contractor$45.0M
236117New Housing For-Sale BuildersBuild homes on your own land for sale$45.0M
236118Residential RemodelersRemodel, add to or repair residential buildings$45.0M
236210Industrial Building ConstructionBuild factories and plants$45.0M
236220Commercial and Institutional Building ConstructionBuild or renovate offices, schools, hospitals, barracks, warehouses$45.0M

Source for sizes: 13 CFR 121.201, as of October 2026.

Federal building work (renovating a VA clinic, an Army reserve center or a courthouse) is coded 236220 in most solicitations. The Census definition covers new work, additions, alterations, maintenance and repairs of commercial and institutional buildings (NAICS 236220). That is why 236220 tends to be the main code for a federal GC even when its jobs are renovations and not ground-up builds.

Here is an example. A three-person GC that mostly does tenant improvements and small renovations for federal agencies would normally pick 236220 as primary. It would add 236118 only if residential remodeling is a real revenue line.

Pitfall: A holding company or "construction business" that just owns subsidiaries doesn't get a construction code automatically. The code belongs to the entity that does the work and gets the receipts.

NAICS Code for Residential Construction vs. Commercial Construction

Residential construction uses 236115–236118, and commercial construction uses 236220. Today all five share a $45.0M size standard (13 CFR 121.201). The difference that matters for bidding is which code agencies actually put on solicitations.

QuestionResidential (236115–236118)Commercial (236220)
Typical federal buyersMilitary family housing, some HUD-funded and tribal housing workNearly every agency's facility renovation and new-build work
Current size standard$45.0M$45.0M
Proposed August 2026 changeMoves to an employee-based standard (proposed, not final)600 employees (proposed, not final)

On August 20, 2026, SBA proposed collapsing nearly 1,000 six-digit size standards into 338 and moving construction to employee-based standards. Under that proposal, 236220 would change from $45M to 600 employees (Thompson Hine; Schoonover & Moriarty). Comments closed September 21, 2026. As of October 2026 it is still a proposal, so the receipts-based numbers in this guide are the ones that apply. Track the docket at Regulations.gov SBA-2026-0199.

Pitfall: Builders sometimes code multifamily work as 236220 because the building "looks commercial." Census treats multifamily housing as residential (236116). Mixed-use buildings are judged by their main purpose. If you're unsure, read the cross-references in the Census definition before you choose.

What Is the NAICS Code for Construction Management and Construction Project Management?

For construction management of commercial and institutional buildings, the code is 236220 if the firm takes on construction responsibility. Census lists "Construction management, commercial and institutional building" as an index entry under 236220 (NAICS 236220 index). A firm that only advises the owner, without holding the trade contracts or the construction risk, usually fits a professional-services code instead.

How to tell which applies:

  • CM at-risk or CM/GC: You hold the subcontracts, guarantee a price and carry schedule risk. Use 236220, or the matching 236/237 code for the type of project.
  • CM-agent or owner's representative with engineering content (reviewing designs, checking technical submittals, inspecting during construction): 541330 Engineering Services. Its Census definition includes "provision of technical services during the construction or installation phase" (NAICS 541330). Size standard: $25.5M (13 CFR 121.201).
  • Project management focused on schedules, budgets and administration, without engineering: 541611 Administrative Management and General Management Consulting Services, with a $24.5M size standard (13 CFR 121.201).

Here is an example. A firm hired by a Navy installation to manage a GC's schedule and pay applications, which never signs a subcontract, would look at 541330 or 541611. A firm that holds a guaranteed maximum price on the same project would use 236220.

Pitfall: Both 541330 and 541611 have lower size ceilings than 236220. A $30M firm that is small under 236220 is other-than-small under 541330's base $25.5M standard. Check before you change codes.

What Is the NAICS Code for Construction Consulting and Construction Consulting Services?

Construction consulting with no hands-on building usually falls under 541330 Engineering Services when the work is technical, or 541611 when it is managerial. Neither is a Sector 23 code, so construction set-asides coded 236/237/238 don't apply to this work.

Steps to place a consulting service

  1. Write one sentence describing what the client pays for. For example: "We review structural drawings for code compliance." This example is illustrative only.
  2. Ask whether engineering judgment is the product. If yes, use 541330. Its definition covers advice, feasibility studies, plans and designs, construction-phase technical services, and inspection of engineering projects (NAICS 541330).
  3. If the product is organizing, planning or administration, use 541611 ($24.5M).
  4. If the product is design of buildings, look at 541310 Architectural Services ($12.5M), which has a much lower ceiling (13 CFR 121.201).
  5. Check the 541330 exceptions. Military and aerospace equipment engineering, Energy Policy Act work and marine engineering each carry a $47.0M standard instead of $25.5M (13 CFR 121.201). Those exceptions only apply when the solicitation says so.

One thing to watch: SBA's August 2026 proposal would remove these 541330 sub-industry exceptions and would move 541611 to a much higher receipts figure under a combined 5416 group (Schoonover & Moriarty). Nothing changes until a final rule is published.

NAICS Code for Construction Cost Estimating

Construction cost estimating sold as a standalone service is indexed by Census under 541990 All Other Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services (Ask Kodiak NAICS index). It has a $19.5M size standard (13 CFR 121.201). Cost engineering done inside a broader engineering engagement fits 541330.

The plan for this guide started with a common assumption that estimating sits under 541350. It doesn't. 541350 is Building Inspection Services, a separate activity with an $11.5M standard (13 CFR 121.201). Use 541350 only if inspection is the main thing you sell.

What you sellBest-fit codeSize standard
Stand-alone quantity takeoffs and cost estimates541990$19.5M
Cost engineering as part of engineering services541330$25.5M
Building inspections541350$11.5M
Estimating as part of your own GC bidsNot a separate code; it's part of 236xxx$45.0M

Here is an example. An estimator who prepares independent government cost estimates (IGCEs) for an agency under a services contract would list 541990, and 541330 if engineers sign the work.

Pitfall: Don't add 541990 just because your GC does estimating internally. You only list a code for services you sell to clients.

NAICS Code for Interior Construction and Specialty Trade Work

Interior construction usually maps to a Specialty Trade Contractor code in the 2383xx group (Building Finishing Contractors). The exact code depends on the trade. A firm that takes responsibility for a whole interior build-out as prime is doing 236220 work instead.

Interior tradeCodeSize standard
Drywall, plaster, insulation238310$19.0M
Painting and wall covering238320$19.0M
Flooring (carpet, vinyl, wood)238330$19.0M
Tile and terrazzo238340$19.0M
Finish carpentry (millwork, cabinets, doors)238350$19.0M
Other finishing work238390$19.0M
Electrical238210$19.0M
Plumbing and HVAC238220$19.0M
Other building equipment (e.g., elevators)238290$22.0M

Sizes: 13 CFR 121.201, as of October 2026.

Here is an example. A drywall and acoustical ceiling firm uses 238310. If it starts taking full office build-outs where it hires the electrician, painter and flooring sub, that revenue becomes 236220 work. Once that share is the largest, its primary code should change.

The 238 codes also change how much you can subcontract on a set-aside. A specialty trade prime may pay non-similarly-situated firms no more than 75% of the contract amount, compared with 85% for general construction. Material costs are excluded in both cases (13 CFR 125.6). For how these limits play out, see our 51 rule checklist.

What Is the NAICS Code for Construction Services and Construction Work (General Catch-All Searches)?

There is no NAICS code called "construction services" or "construction work." Those phrases map to whichever building, civil or specialty-trade code matches the actual scope. When a contracting officer buys "construction services," they still have to pick one 6-digit code.

Steps to find the code for a vague scope

  1. List the work items in the scope (for example: demolition, new roof, HVAC replacement, interior finishes).
  2. Estimate each item's share of contract value. Procurements are classified by "the component which accounts for the greatest percentage of contract value" (13 CFR 121.402).
  3. Code the largest component. A job that is 70% roofing is coded 238160. A job with many trades under one prime is usually coded 236220.
  4. Check facility-maintenance bundles. If the scope is ongoing building operations, it may be coded 561210 Facilities Support Services ($47.0M). The SBA footnote says that if one specific industry makes up 50% or more of the value, that industry's code applies instead (13 CFR 121.201).

Pitfall: Typing "construction" into the Census search returns dozens of results. Search for the specific activity ("site preparation," "water main," "roof") instead. Site preparation is 238910 ($19.0M), and water and sewer line work is 237110 ($45.0M).

How Your NAICS Code Choice Changes Your SBA Size Standard and Set-Aside Eligibility

For each contract, the size standard you must meet belongs to the NAICS code in that solicitation. The contracting officer designates "the single NAICS code which best describes the principal purpose" of the acquisition (13 CFR 121.402). In Sector 23, that code's ceiling ranges from $19.0M to $45.0M.

Your average annual receipts (example)Small under 238xxx ($19M)?Small under 237990 dredging ($37M)?Small under 236220 ($45M)?
$12MYesYesYes
$21MNo (except 238290 at $22M)YesYes
$40MNoNoYes
$48MNoNoNo

The thresholds come from 13 CFR 121.201. The receipt amounts are examples.

What this means for your bids:

  • SAM.gov is checked per code. SAM profiles show small business status against the size standards. After SBA changed the table, firms had to update their SAM registrations before their status refreshed (SBA). If a code isn't in your profile, you can't certify as small under it.
  • Dredging has an extra test. To count as small on a dredging procurement, you and similarly situated subcontractors must perform at least 40% of the volume dredged with your own equipment or equipment owned by another small dredging concern (13 CFR 121.201).
  • Set-aside type sits on top of size. 8(a), WOSB, HUBZone and SDVOSB set-asides all require you to be small under the solicitation's code first. See our SBA size standards by NAICS guide and the total vs partial set-aside checklist.

If the solicitation's code looks wrong

Any interested party adversely affected by a NAICS code designation may appeal to SBA's Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA). The appeal must be filed within 10 calendar days after the solicitation (or the amendment changing the code) is issued. Late appeals are dismissed. A timely appeal makes the contracting officer stay the closing date (13 CFR 121.1103).

Here is an example. A renovation that is mostly HVAC replacement is coded 236220 ($45M). A $20M HVAC contractor is small under either code. But if larger general contractors are using 236220 to compete against small mechanical firms, a 238220 code would narrow the field to firms under $19M. Whether an appeal is worth filing depends on whether the scope really is mostly one trade. It is not a tactic for removing competitors.

Before an RFP comes out, you can raise a coding concern informally. Our sources sought response template shows where to suggest a NAICS code.

Next steps

Start with your own revenue figures. Most code mistakes come from guessing which code fits instead of measuring where your receipts come from.

Today, on your own:

  1. Export last fiscal year's revenue by job type, calculate the share for each code, and set the largest as your primary.
  2. Calculate your 5-year average annual receipts, including affiliates, and compare it with every code you plan to list in the SBA table.
  3. Open SAM.gov, go to Update Entity Registration, then Goods and Services, and remove any codes you can't perform or aren't small under.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) offer government contracting counseling, including NAICS selection and SAM.gov review, generally at no cost (as of October 2026; check the official page). This suits first-time bidders and firms clearly under the thresholds. It is less useful if you need legal advice on an affiliation or size protest question, because counselors are not your lawyers, and appointment wait times vary by location.
  • A government contracts attorney makes sense when your receipts are within a few million dollars of a threshold, or when you are considering an OHA NAICS appeal with its 10-day deadline. Fees vary widely and are usually hourly, so get a written estimate first. A firm well below every relevant standard usually doesn't need one.

FAQ

What is the NAICS code for a construction company?

Most construction companies that take responsibility for whole buildings use 236220 for commercial and institutional work or 236115–236118 for residential work. Each of these has a $45.0M size standard (13 CFR 121.201). Trade-focused companies use a 238xxx code, and civil firms use a 237xxx code. Your primary code should match your largest source of receipts.

What is the NAICS code for interior construction?

Interior finish trades fall under Specialty Trade Contractors: 238310 for drywall, 238320 for painting, 238330 for flooring, 238340 for tile and 238350 for finish carpentry. Most have a $19.0M standard (13 CFR 121.201). If you manage the whole interior build-out as prime, that work is 236220.

What is the NAICS code for commercial construction?

Commercial construction is 236220, Commercial and Institutional Building Construction. It covers new work, additions, alterations, maintenance and repairs (NAICS 236220). Its current size standard is $45.0M. SBA's August 2026 proposal would change it to 600 employees, but that is not final.

What is the NAICS code for construction project management?

If you hold the construction contracts and carry the risk, Census indexes construction management of commercial buildings under 236220. If you only manage or advise for the owner, 541330 ($25.5M) or 541611 ($24.5M) usually fits better (13 CFR 121.201).

What is the NAICS code for construction work?

"Construction work" doesn't have its own code. The code depends on the largest component of the work by contract value (13 CFR 121.402). Look up the specific activity in the Census NAICS search and use that 6-digit code.
