item.title: NAICS Code for Consulting: 2026 Size Table and Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: NAICS code for consulting: match 541611, 541613, 541618, 541690, 541512 or 541990 to your service, with each SBA size standard and SAM.gov steps.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

No single NAICS code covers all consulting. Most general business and management consulting uses 541611 (Administrative Management and General Management Consulting Services), and its SBA size standard is $24.5 million in average annual receipts (GSA OASIS+ NAICS table, as of October 2026). Marketing, HR, logistics, safety, environmental and IT consulting each have their own codes and limits, from $19.0M to $34.0M. Pick the code that matches the service that brings in most of your revenue. Then check that your receipts are under that code's limit.

Which option is right for you?

Choose your primary code based on what clients mostly pay you for. Your company's name, structure and size don't decide it.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner: you advise on strategy, operations, budgeting or organization541611 ($24.5M)SBA size standards tool
You mostly do marketing strategy, pricing or sales advice541613 ($19.0M)GSA OASIS+ NAICS table
You design and integrate IT systems541512 ($34.0M)13 CFR 121.201 table
You advise on workplace safety, security or other technical topics541690 ($19.0M)NAICS 541690 index
Your daily work is answering federal solicitations in several areasPrimary code plus secondary codes in SAM.govSAM.gov → Entity Registrations
You're on a tight budget and want free helpFree counseling from an APEX Accelerator before you registerAPEX Accelerators

What Is the NAICS Code for Consulting Services?

Most consulting services use 541611, but there are about ten consulting codes. Each one has its own SBA size standard.

The consulting codes sit in NAICS industry group 5416 (Management, Scientific, and Technical Consulting Services). A few related professional-services codes sit next to it. The table below shows the receipts-based limits SBA uses now. The figures come from the regulation (13 CFR 121.201 via Cornell LII) and from GSA's OASIS+ table (GSA). SBA's downloadable table has an effective date of March 17, 2023 (SBA). All figures are as of October 2026; check the official page before you bid.

NAICSTitleTypical consulting workSBA size standard
541611Administrative Management & General Management ConsultingStrategy, org planning, budgeting, operations$24.5M
541612Human Resources ConsultingCompensation, HR policy, workforce planning$29.0M
541613Marketing ConsultingMarketing plans, pricing, sales forecasting$19.0M
541614Process, Physical Distribution & Logistics ConsultingSupply chain, inventory, distribution$20.0M
541618Other Management ConsultingTelecom and utilities management consulting$19.0M
541620Environmental ConsultingEnvironmental compliance advice$19.0M
541690Other Scientific & Technical ConsultingSafety, security, energy, agricultural consulting$19.0M
541990All Other Professional, Scientific & Technical ServicesCatch-all professional services$19.5M
541512Computer Systems Design ServicesIT systems integration and design$34.0M
541330Engineering ServicesEngineering-led consulting$25.5M (some exceptions $47.0M)
611430Professional & Management Development TrainingLeadership training, workshops$15.0M

Some of these codes get mixed up often. 541618 is not a general "other consulting" code for any kind of advice. Its index entries are telecommunications and utilities management consulting (NAICS 541618). 541990 is also narrower than its name suggests. Its definition specifically leaves out consulting, along with legal, accounting, engineering and computer systems design. Its examples include appraisal, arbitration and weather forecasting (NAICS 541990). You'll still see 541990 on solicitations because agencies use it for broad contract vehicles. For example, GSA uses 541990 as the administrative NAICS on all six OASIS+ solicitations (GSA).

Before you choose, read each code's official description in the Census Bureau's NAICS search at census.gov/naics. SAM.gov uses the 2022 NAICS edition (Federal Filing), so search the 2022 year.

What Is the Best NAICS Code for Consulting?

The best code is the most specific one that matches your main revenue-earning service. The broadest code and the most popular code are not automatically the right ones.

SBA counts you as small or not small for a particular NAICS code. When you bid, the code that matters is the one the contracting officer put on that solicitation. A contracting officer chooses one code per solicitation. They look at the NAICS Manual descriptions, the statement of work, and which part of the contract is worth the most money (13 CFR 121.402). So your primary code in SAM.gov describes your business. The code on the solicitation decides your eligibility for that bid.

Use this checklist to pick your primary code:

  1. List what you billed for in the last 12–24 months. For example, a firm might list "operations reviews 60%, marketing plans 25%, staff workshops 15%."
  2. Find the activity with the largest share. In that example it's operations reviews, which points to 541611.
  3. Search that activity at census.gov/naics with the year set to 2022, then read the definition and its "excludes" notes.
  4. Compare the code with the size standard for each realistic alternative. A firm earning $21M a year is small under 541611 ($24.5M) but not small under 541613 ($19.0M).
  5. Look at what agencies actually put on solicitations for your work. On SAM.gov, go to Search → Contract Opportunities and filter by NAICS Code. If buyers keep assigning 541611 to work like yours, add it.
  6. Enter that code as your primary NAICS in SAM.gov, and list the others as secondary codes.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Choosing a code only because its size limit is higher. Your primary code should describe what you actually do. In any case, your eligibility on each bid depends on the solicitation's code, not your primary one.
  • Leaving out codes that buyers actually use. If agencies post your kind of work under 541990 or 541618, add those as secondary codes so you show up in their searches. You still have to be under each code's size standard to bid as small under it.
  • Using an outdated code. NAICS changes every five years. If a code won't save in SAM.gov, check that it exists in the 2022 edition (Federal Filing).

Our SBA size standards by NAICS guide covers how to check the full table and how size appeals work.

What Is the NAICS Code for Management Consulting?

Management consulting is NAICS 541611. Its SBA size standard is $24.5 million in average annual receipts (as of October 2026).

The official description of 541611 covers advice to organizations on "strategic and organizational planning, financial planning and budgeting, marketing objectives and policies, human resource policies, and production scheduling" (NAICS 541611). Most management consultants who work across several of those areas belong here.

If one specialty clearly brings in most of your revenue, a sibling code fits better:

  • Mostly HR work, such as compensation studies or HR policy: 541612, $29.0M.
  • Mostly logistics or supply chain work: 541614, $20.0M.
  • Management consulting only for telecom or utility clients: 541618, $19.0M.

All figures are from GSA, as of October 2026.

For example, take a firm whose federal work is mostly program-office reviews, process redesign and budget formulation support. 541611 is its natural primary code. If that firm's five-year average receipts are $18M, it is small under 541611, 541612 and 541614. It is also small under the $19.0M codes, but just barely.

Agencies often use 541611 for advisory and assistance services. Your capability statement should list it with the same wording used in the statements of work you're targeting.

What Is the NAICS Code for Marketing Consulting?

Marketing consulting is NAICS 541613 (Marketing Consulting Services). Its size standard is $19.0 million, which is lower than the $24.5M limit for 541611.

541613 covers advice on "developing marketing objectives and policies, sales forecasting, new product developing and pricing" (NAICS 541613). Its cross-references send two nearby services elsewhere. Public relations planning goes to 541820, and market research and polling go to 541910 (NAICS 541613). Their limits are $19.0M and $22.5M (13 CFR 121.201).

If most revenue comes from…CodeSize standard
Marketing strategy, pricing, go-to-market advice541613$19.0M
Surveys, focus groups, polling541910$22.5M
PR planning and media relations541820$19.0M

For example, a firm that runs recruitment-marketing strategy for an agency and also fields surveys would compare the revenue from each. If the surveys are the larger share, 541910 is the better primary code.

One mistake to watch for: a firm with $20M in receipts that registers 541613 as primary can lose small-business status on marketing contracts it could have won as a 541910 firm. That is only true if research is honestly its main activity. The code has to describe the actual work, and you can't pick it to fit a size limit.

What Is the NAICS Code for Technology Consulting?

Technology and IT consulting usually falls under 541512 (Computer Systems Design Services), with a $34.0 million size standard. 541618 is not the code for general IT advice.

541512 covers "planning and designing computer systems that integrate computer hardware, software, and communication technologies." Its index entries include "computer systems integration design consulting" (NAICS 541512). Three related IT codes also share the $34.0M limit: 541511 (Custom Computer Programming), 541512 itself, and 541519 (Other Computer Related Services). 541513 (Computer Facilities Management) is $37.0M (13 CFR 121.201).

Core serviceCodeSize standard
IT architecture, systems integration, cloud design541512$34.0M
Custom software development541511$34.0M
Other IT services (e.g., disaster recovery)541519$34.0M
IT reselling with value-added services (ITVAR exception)541519 exception150 employees
Telecom management consulting (non-design)541618$19.0M
IT governance or strategy with no systems workOften 541611$24.5M

Watch out for the ITVAR exception. It uses a 150-employee limit instead of receipts. It applies to contracts for multi-vendor hardware and software where value-added services make up 15–50% of the contract price (13 CFR 121.201). If you mainly resell licenses, the employee test is the one that counts on those bids.

What Is the NAICS Code for Safety Consulting?

Safety consulting is listed under NAICS 541690 (Other Scientific and Technical Consulting Services), with a $19.0 million size standard. It is not under 541990.

The Census index lists "safety consulting services" and "occupational health and safety consulting services" as entries under 541690. Security consulting and product quality consulting are listed there too (NAICS 541690; Statistics Canada NAICS 2022 examples). The 541690 limit is $19.0M (GSA).

Two other codes can apply to safety work:

  • Environmental focus (air permits, contamination, NEPA-type compliance advice): 541620 Environmental Consulting, $19.0M.
  • Engineering-led work (stamped designs, fire protection engineering): 541330 Engineering Services, $25.5M. Certain military, aerospace, Energy Policy Act and marine engineering exceptions are $47.0M (13 CFR 121.201).

For example, a firm that writes OSHA compliance programs and runs site safety audits for a VA medical center fits 541690. If the same firm mostly designs fire suppression systems under a professional engineer's seal, 541330 fits better.

A common mistake is listing only 541990 because it sounds broad. Agencies searching SAM.gov for safety consultants filter by 541690, so you'd be missing from those results. List 541690 first, and add 541990 only if you also do work that its index actually covers.

What Is the NAICS Code for Consulting and Coaching?

Consulting with some coaching mixed in usually stays under 541611. Training-led coaching uses 611430, and life coaching for individuals is listed under 812990.

There is no code just for "coaching." Three NAICS listings come close:

  • 611430 Professional and Management Development Training covers structured leadership and professional development. Its size standard is $15.0M (13 CFR 121.201).
  • 812990 All Other Personal Services has "life coach services" as an index entry (Ask Kodiak NAICS index). It rarely fits federal work, which is usually sold to organizations, not to individuals.
  • 541611 fits when the coaching supports advisory work you're paid for, such as executive coaching during a reorganization.

To decide:

  1. Split last year's revenue into advice (assessments, recommendations, plans) and instruction (workshops, curriculum, cohort programs).
  2. If advice is the larger share, make 541611 primary and add 611430 as secondary.
  3. If instruction is the larger share, make 611430 primary. Remember its $15.0M limit is the lowest in this guide.
  4. Check what agencies post. Leadership development for federal supervisors is often posted as training, so search Contract Opportunities for both codes before you decide.

A common mistake is putting "coaching" in your capability statement while your SAM.gov codes are all 5416 consulting codes. Buyers filtering for 611430 won't find you. Make the codes and your description match.

NAICS Code for Small Business Consulting

Most small business consultants use 541611. You count as small under it if your average annual receipts are below $24.5 million (as of October 2026).

"Small business consulting" is not a separate NAICS industry. It's management consulting where the clients happen to be small firms, so 541611 applies. One related code is easy to mix up with it: 541211/541219 for bookkeeping and accounting-led advice. Check the Census search if most of your billable work is tax or accounting.

SBA's test uses receipts, not profit. For a firm in business five or more years, it is "total receipts of the concern over its most recently completed 5 fiscal years divided by 5." Receipts mean total income plus cost of goods sold. Subcontractor costs and reimbursed purchases cannot be excluded, and you must add in your affiliates' receipts (13 CFR 121.104). A firm that has been operating less than five years annualizes its receipts by weeks in business (13 CFR 121.104).

Example only, with made-up numbers:

Fiscal yearReceipts (example)
2021$14.0M
2022$18.0M
2023$22.0M
2024$27.0M
2025$30.0M
5-year average$22.2M

At $22.2M, this firm is small under 541611 ($24.5M) and 541612 ($29.0M). It is not small under 541613, 541618 or 541690 ($19.0M each). Its last two years were above $24.5M, but the five-year average keeps it small under 541611 for now.

You'll also see much bigger numbers for these codes in the news. On August 20, 2026, SBA proposed a major overhaul that would merge size standards into 338 groups and set a new minimum of $30.6M in receipts (Federal Register; Thompson Hine). Under the proposal, 541611 would go from $24.5M to $295M, and 541512 from $34M to $531M (Thompson Hine). The comment period was extended to November 20, 2026 (SmallGovCon via Wifcon). A separate August 2025 inflation proposal has also not been finalized (National Law Review). Until SBA publishes a final rule with an effective date, use the current figures in this guide.

NAICS Code for Consulting Firm vs Freelance Consultant

Your business structure doesn't change your NAICS code. A solo LLC and a 200-person firm doing the same work use the same code.

NAICS classifies a business by what it is "primarily engaged in." The code descriptions don't mention entity type or headcount (NAICS 541611). The differences between a solo consultant and a firm show up elsewhere:

  • Size. A one-person shop with $400K in receipts is small under every code in this guide. A growing firm has to recheck its five-year average every year.
  • Affiliation. If you also own part of another company, its receipts may count toward your size (13 CFR 121.104).
  • Teaming. Freelancers often start as subcontractors. When you sub, the prime decides which work you do, but your size is still measured against the solicitation's NAICS code.

For example, a former agency analyst who sets up as a single-member LLC selling program evaluation uses 541611, just as a large firm would. Picking 541990 "because I'm a freelancer" is a mistake.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Copying an old employer's codes. Their mix of services isn't yours. Build your list from your own revenue.
  • Not registering because you're "too small." You can't be awarded federal contracts without an active SAM.gov registration. Our SAM.gov registration guide walks through it, from getting a UEI to an active registration.

How to add or change your consulting NAICS codes in SAM.gov

These are the steps for an existing registration (Federal Filing):

  1. Go to SAM.gov, click Sign In, and log in with Login.gov.
  2. Open Entity Registrations → Existing Entity Registrations and select your entity.
  3. Click Update Entity.
  4. Go to Goods and Services, then enter your NAICS codes and mark one as Primary.
  5. Check the small business status SAM shows next to each code, then submit. Your size status for each code comes from the receipts you entered in the registration.

When the code on a solicitation looks wrong

Each solicitation has one code (13 CFR 121.402). If the code doesn't match the statement of work, you can appeal to SBA's Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA). The designation is final unless someone appeals in time (13 CFR 121.402). The deadline is short, usually 10 calendar days after the solicitation is issued (13 CFR 134.304). Before you consider an appeal, ask the contracting officer about the code. Answering a sources sought notice is a good, low-risk time to raise it.

Next steps

You can do the first two steps below today. Both are free.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Split last year's revenue by service and match the largest share to a code from the table at the top.
  2. Enter that code in the SBA size standards tool along with your five-year average receipts.
  3. Search SAM.gov Contract Opportunities by that code. Save three recent notices so you can see how agencies describe the work.

If you'd rather have help:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) give free, one-on-one help with NAICS selection, SAM.gov and bid readiness (apexaccelerators.us). They're a good fit for first-time bidders. Limitation: counselors don't act as your lawyer, and wait times differ by location. They're not the right choice if you need a size protest or NAICS appeal filed under a deadline.
  • A government contracts attorney is the right call for a size protest, an OHA NAICS appeal, or affiliation questions after an acquisition. Fees vary by firm and matter (as of October 2026; ask for a written quote). Don't hire one just to pick a primary code; free counseling covers that.

Related guides on this site:

  • SBA Size Standards by NAICS: 2026 Table, Steps & Appeals
  • SAM.gov Registration Guide: 7 Steps From UEI to Active
  • How to Bid on Government Contracts: 7 Steps, 2026 Costs

FAQ

What is the NAICS number for consulting?

The most common NAICS number for consulting is 541611, Administrative Management and General Management Consulting Services. Its size standard is $24.5M. Specialized consulting has its own numbers: 541612 (HR), 541613 (marketing), 541614 (logistics), 541618 (telecom/utilities management), 541620 (environmental), and 541690 (scientific and technical, including safety).

What is the NAICS code for consulting business?

A consulting business uses the code for the service that brings in most of its revenue. For general business advisory firms, that's 541611. Whether you're an LLC, an S-corp or a sole proprietor doesn't matter. Only the activity does.

Naics code for consulting work

Consulting work on a federal contract is classified by the code the contracting officer puts on the solicitation. They choose based on the statement of work and the part of the contract worth the most (13 CFR 121.402). Your size is measured against that code's standard, even if your primary code is different.

What is the NAICS code for consulting services?

Consulting services are grouped under NAICS 5416, Management, Scientific, and Technical Consulting Services. As of October 2026, the six-digit codes in that group have size standards from $19.0M to $29.0M. IT consulting that includes systems design falls under 541512 instead, with a $34.0M limit.

item.description: How to use the SBA HUBZone map in 2026: check an address, spot expired redesignated areas, read your result, and find HUBZone set-asides on SAM.gov.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The HUBZone map is SBA's free online tool at maps.certify.sba.gov/hubzone/map. You type in a street address or GPS coordinates, and it tells you whether that spot sits inside a Historically Underutilized Business Zone (SBA map help). In 2026 a clean result needs one more check. Every "Redesignated Area" created by the 2023 map update expired on July 1, 2026 (SBA map help), so read the designation type and expiration date on the result, then confirm that real HUBZone set-asides exist on SAM.gov in your line of work.

Which option is right for you?

Your first step depends on where you are now. The table gives you a starting point and the page to open.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, no SBA certification yet, just curious if your office qualifiesRun one address check on the official mapSBA HUBZone Map
Already certified, bidding regularly (daily work use)Re-check your principal office and every employee address against the July 1, 2026 expirationSBA HUBZone Map, then MySBA Certifications
Not registered on SAM.gov yetGet an active SAM.gov registration before you think about certificationSAM.gov and our SAM.gov registration guide
Tight budget, want free helpUse the free map plus a free APEX Accelerator counselorAPEX Accelerators
Deciding if HUBZone is worth the effort at allCount live HUBZone set-asides in your NAICS code firstSAM.gov HUBZone set-aside search

Why this order? For a beginner the map costs nothing and needs no account (DLA HUBZone overview). Certified firms face the July 2026 expiration risk right now. And if SAM.gov shows almost no HUBZone work in your industry, that tells you more about the program's value to you than any map result.

What is a HUBZone Map?

The HUBZone Map is SBA's online GIS tool for checking whether an address falls in a Historically Underutilized Business Zone. That answer decides whether a business located there can use the HUBZone federal contracting program.

It sits at maps.certify.sba.gov/hubzone/map, on the same SBA certification platform that handles HUBZone applications. According to SBA's map help page, you can:

  • search by street address, with autocomplete suggestions as you type
  • search by GPS coordinates in "latitude, longitude" format, for example 38.93655, -77.01993, with no degree symbol and a minus sign for negative values
  • switch base maps between "Standard," "Light Gray" and "Satellite"
  • open the legend to see every HUBZone type with its own color and pattern
  • use "My Location" (with browser permission) to check where you're standing
  • print the result for your records

The map shows six designation types: Census Tract, County, Indian Land, Redesignated Area, Disaster Area and Governor-Designated Covered Area (SBA map help). Each type follows different rules about how long it lasts, which is why the type matters as much as the yes/no answer.

The common mistake is to treat the map as a certification. It isn't one. It only tells you about a location. To win HUBZone contracts the business also has to be small, at least 51% owned and controlled by U.S. citizens (or certain tribal, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian or cooperative owners), keep its principal office in a HUBZone, and have at least 35% of its employees living in a HUBZone (SBA HUBZone program).

What is a HUBZone Area?

A HUBZone area is a census tract, county, Indian land, or special-status area that meets SBA's economic distress criteria. Businesses based and staffed there can compete for HUBZone contracts.

The legal definitions are in 13 CFR 126.103. The table below puts them next to the map labels, because the duration column is what catches people out.

Map labelWhat qualifies itHow long it lasts
Census Tract (Qualified Census Tract)Designated by HUD: 50%+ of households earn under 60% of area median income, or the poverty rate is 25%+Until the next five-year map update (next one July 2028)
County (Qualified Non-Metropolitan County)Non-metro county with median household income under 80% of the state median, unemployment at 140%+ of the national or state average, or a Difficult Development AreaUntil the next five-year map update
Indian LandInside an Indian Reservation, Indian Country, or Oklahoma-specific definitionsOngoing
Redesignated AreaA tract or county that stopped qualifying3 years from the date it lost status (2023 ones ended July 1, 2026)
Disaster Area (Qualified Disaster Area)Tract or non-metro county in a presidentially declared major disaster area that lost status within the prior 5 yearsFrom the declaration date until SBA updates the map
Governor-Designated Covered AreaPetitioned by a governor and approved by SBA; outside urbanized areas, population of 50,000 or less, unemployment at 120%+ of averageExpires on its own schedule, shown on the map
Qualified Base Closure AreaFormer military base closure areaAt least 8 years from designation

Sources: 13 CFR 126.103, SBA map help.

The county test only applies to non-metropolitan counties. So if your office is in a metro county, such as most suburbs of a major city, only census tracts (or one of the special types) can make your address qualify. Neighboring blocks can get different answers.

What is a HUBZone?

HUBZone stands for Historically Underutilized Business Zone. It's an SBA program that gives small businesses located in and employing residents of distressed areas preferred access to federal contracts.

According to SBA and FAR subpart 19.13, as of October 2026 the program works like this:

  • Government-wide goal: agencies aim to award 3% of federal contracting dollars to HUBZone firms.
  • Set-asides: a contracting officer can restrict a competition to HUBZone firms when there's a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more of them at a fair market price (FAR 19.1305).
  • Sole-source awards: allowed up to $8.5 million for manufacturing NAICS codes and $5.5 million for all other NAICS codes, options included (FAR 19.1306).
  • Price evaluation preference: in full and open competition, offers from non-HUBZone firms get a 10% factor added when the agency compares prices against a HUBZone offer (FAR 19.1307).
  • Recertification: every three years, submitted in the 90 calendar days before your certification anniversary (13 CFR 126.500).

Here's an example, with numbers made up for illustration. A HUBZone firm bids $1,000,000 in a full-and-open competition. A large business bids $950,000. With the 10% factor, the large business's price is evaluated as $1,045,000, so the HUBZone firm comes out lower on price. FAR 19.1307 lists exceptions, so read that section before you count on the preference.

The employee test matters as much as the office address. Under SBA's December 2024 final rule, effective January 16, 2025, an employee counts as a HUBZone resident after living in a HUBZone for 90 days, down from 180. The 35% residency requirement stayed the same (PilieroMazza summary of the rule). Size still decides everything as well, so check your NAICS code in our SBA size standards guide.

How to Use the HUBZone Map for a 2026 Eligibility Check

Enter a full street address, not just a city or ZIP code, because eligibility follows census tract lines that can change block by block. Then read the result and the legend together.

Step-by-step

  1. Open maps.certify.sba.gov/hubzone/map. You don't need an account.
  2. Click the search bar and type the full address: number, street, city, state. Pick the matching autocomplete suggestion (SBA map help).
  3. Press Enter or click the magnifying glass icon.
  4. Read the result panel. It shows whether the location is qualified and which designation type applies.
  5. If the address is rural or brand new and the geocoder can't find it, clear the field with the "x" and search by coordinates in latitude, longitude format.
  6. Switch the base map to "Light Gray." SBA says it gives a clearer view than "Standard," which helps when your pin sits near a tract boundary.
  7. Open the legend and check that the color under your pin matches the type in the result panel.
  8. If the type is Redesignated Area, Disaster Area or Governor-Designated Covered Area, write down the expiration date (see the next section).
  9. Print the result. The map has a print option for documentation (SBA map help).
  10. Repeat for every employee's home address, not just the office. The 35% test depends on where people live.

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeWhy it's wrongFix
Searching a ZIP codeZIP codes don't follow census tract linesUse the full street address or coordinates
Checking only the office35% of employees must live in a HUBZoneCheck every employee address and keep a dated list
Checking a virtual office or mailbox addressThe principal office is where the most employees work, and you need a lease or deed at least 30 days old with at least 60 days left (13 CFR 126.103)Check the address where your team actually works
Reading "qualified" without the typeA Redesignated or Disaster Area can expireAlways note the type and any date
Trusting a third-party mapCopies can lag behind SBA's dataUse only maps.certify.sba.gov

How to Confirm Redesignated-Area Expiration Dates on the HUBZone Map

A redesignated HUBZone area keeps its status for three years after losing its original qualification, and the map shows its expiration date. Every redesignated area from the July 2023 update expired on July 1, 2026.

SBA's map help says tracts and counties that lose status "remain qualified for three years," and that the map displays expiration dates for them. The regulation counts those three years from the date the area stopped qualifying (13 CFR 126.103). SBA also says it would update the map in 2026 to remove expiring Redesignated Areas, and that Disaster and Governor-designated areas can expire at any time of year (SBA map help).

How to check

  1. Search the address as described above.
  2. In the result panel, find the designation type. If it says Redesignated Area, look for the expiration date next to it.
  3. Compare that date with today (October 2026). A date of July 1, 2026 or earlier means the area no longer counts, even if the map hasn't caught up yet.
  4. Toggle the legend and turn off the Redesignated Area layer if you can. If your pin no longer sits on any other qualified color, the address doesn't qualify on its own.
  5. Do the same check for Disaster Area and Governor-Designated Covered Area results, since those expire on their own schedules.
  6. Log in to MySBA Certifications and compare your company profile with what the map shows now.

Why this matters even if your certification says "active"

Since January 16, 2025, a firm has to be an eligible HUBZone small business on the date it submits an offer for a HUBZone contract, not just on its certification date (PilieroMazza; FAR 19.1304). A firm can therefore show "active" in SBA's system and still submit an ineligible offer if its office or 35% residency depended on an expired area (OpenGrants, July 2026).

Two related rules come up often:

  • Legacy employees. A firm can count up to four "legacy" HUBZone employees as long as it has at least one current HUBZone resident employee. But someone who first qualified by living in a Redesignated Area or Disaster Area can never be a legacy employee, and anyone who worked under 30 hours a week at any point is excluded (PilieroMazza).
  • Attempt to maintain. While you're performing a HUBZone contract, you have to make documented efforts (job ads, written offers, job fairs) to stay at 35%. Falling below 20% counts as failing that requirement (13 CFR 126.103).

Pitfall: don't expect a quick fix from the map. SBA won't update Qualified Census Tracts and Counties again until July 2028 (SBA map help), so an office that lost status in July 2026 won't get it back from new data any time soon. Your realistic options are moving the office, hiring HUBZone residents, or pausing HUBZone-only bids.

How to Read Your HUBZone Map Certification Result

The map result gives you three things to record: qualified or not, the designation type, and any expiration date. That's your location evidence for an SBA application, a recertification, and your own bid-day eligibility check.

One correction to a common belief: you don't get HUBZone status by checking a box in SAM.gov. You apply, and later recertify every three years, through MySBA Certifications (SBA; 13 CFR 126.500). You still need an active SAM.gov registration, and our SAM.gov registration guide covers that.

How to turn the result into a usable record

  1. Save the printed map result (or a PDF of the print view) with the date in the file name.
  2. Copy the designation type and any expiration date into a simple log with these columns: address, office or employee, type, expiration, date checked.
  3. For employees, add their move-in date. Someone becomes a HUBZone resident after 90 days at that address (PilieroMazza).
  4. Calculate your residency share: HUBZone-resident employees ÷ total employees. It has to be at least 35%.
  5. Re-run steps 1–4 before each HUBZone offer, since eligibility is tested on the offer date.
  6. Put your recertification window on the calendar: the 90 days before your three-year anniversary. If you miss it, SBA decertifies you, but it will reinstate you if you recertify within 30 days of the end of your eligibility period (13 CFR 126.500).

Example of reading a result (illustrative)

Take a 10-person firm with these sample results:

  • Office: "Census Tract," no expiration. That qualifies through July 2028 at least.
  • Employees: 3 in Census Tracts, 1 in a "Redesignated Area" that expired July 1, 2026, and 6 outside any HUBZone.

Before July 2026 it had 4 of 10, or 40%. Now it has 3 of 10, or 30%, which is below 35%. On bid day this firm wouldn't meet the residency requirement, even though its SBA status still shows active. One more HUBZone-resident hire who has lived at their address for 90 days would bring it to 4 of 11, about 36%.

SBA also runs a program examination of each certified firm at least once every three years, and it can do them more often based on risk (13 CFR 126.500). A dated log like the one above is what you'd show an examiner.

HUBZone Map by State: Virginia, Georgia, and Maryland Examples

There's no reliable state-level HUBZone list for Virginia, Georgia, Maryland or any other state. Check each address on the live map, because qualification is set tract by tract and some types expire.

People search "HUBZone map Virginia" or "HUBZone map Maryland" hoping for a list of qualified cities. SBA's tool doesn't work that way: it answers one location at a time (SBA map help). Here's how the rules play out in common situations in these three states. These are examples of the logic, not claims about specific addresses.

  • Metro suburbs (for example Northern Virginia, the Atlanta metro, or suburban Maryland around Baltimore and Washington). These counties are metropolitan, so the non-metro county test can't apply. Only Qualified Census Tracts or special types can qualify an address (13 CFR 126.103). Expect a patchwork where one block qualifies and the next doesn't.
  • Rural counties (for example parts of southwest Virginia, south Georgia, or Maryland's Eastern Shore). A whole non-metro county can qualify on income or unemployment, so one county result may cover all your employees. Still confirm each one, because a county that lost status in 2023 would have been a Redesignated Area and expired on July 1, 2026.
  • Areas hit by federally declared disasters. A Disaster Area designation can make an address qualify for a while. Write down how long it lasts, because it ends when SBA updates the map (13 CFR 126.103).

Pitfalls: state agencies, local chambers and consultants sometimes post PDF maps or county lists. Treat those as background reading only. Look at the date on any such document. If it was made before July 1, 2026, it may still show expired Redesignated Areas. If your employees live across a state line (DC, Maryland and Virginia are a classic case), check each home address on its own. The map doesn't care about state borders.

HUBZone Map 2025 vs 2026: What Changed

The main change from 2025 to 2026 is that all Redesignated Areas from the 2023 update expired on July 1, 2026. The underlying census tracts and counties stay the same until July 2028.

SBA now updates Qualified Census Tracts and Qualified Non-Metropolitan Counties on a five-year cycle. The current map took effect in July 2023, and the next full update is scheduled for July 2028 (SBA map help). The July 2023 update used 2020 Census-based data, and areas that dropped out got the three-year Redesignated status that just ended (Ward & Berry summary via search).

Item20252026 (as of October 2026)
Census Tracts and non-metro Counties2023 mapSame 2023 map (no change until July 2028)
Redesignated Areas from 2023 updateStill counted as HUBZonesExpired July 1, 2026
Disaster and Governor-designated areasAdded and expired during the yearAdded and expired during the year
RecertificationTriennial (rule effective Jan 16, 2025)Triennial
Eligibility test for HUBZone offersDate of offer (from Jan 16, 2025)Date of offer
Employee residency period90 days (from Jan 16, 2025)90 days

Sources: SBA map help, 13 CFR 126.500, PilieroMazza.

Pitfall: reusing a 2025 screenshot. A 2025 printout showing "Redesignated Area" was accurate then, but it doesn't help you now. Make a fresh check and file it with this year's date.

HUBZone Set-Aside: Finding Live Contract Opportunities on SAM.gov

Once the map confirms your eligibility, search SAM.gov Contract Opportunities filtered to HUBZone set-asides to see what you could actually bid on. Most map guides skip this step.

SAM.gov uses two HUBZone set-aside codes, per the GSA Get Opportunities API documentation:

  • HZC: "Historically Underutilized Business (HUBZone) Set-Aside (FAR 19.13)"
  • HZS: "Historically Underutilized Business (HUBZone) Sole Source (FAR 19.13)"

Steps

  1. Open the prefiltered SAM.gov search. The setAside=HZC part of the URL applies the HUBZone Set-Aside filter for you.
  2. In the left filter panel, keep the status on active notices so expired ones don't clutter your results.
  3. Under Notice Type, choose "Solicitation" and "Combined Synopsis/Solicitation" for things you can bid on now. Add "Sources Sought" if you want to influence future set-asides.
  4. Enter your primary NAICS code in the NAICS filter.
  5. Optionally narrow by place of performance (state or ZIP code).
  6. Open a notice and confirm that its "Set Aside" field says HUBZone. Then read the solicitation's eligibility clauses.
  7. Check the notice's NAICS size standard against your firm's size.
  8. If you're logged in, save the search so you can run it again quickly.

How to use what you find

Count the results. If you see few HUBZone notices in your NAICS code across a year, many of your opportunities may still come through total small business set-asides (see total vs partial small business set-asides) or the 10% price preference in open competitions. Sources sought notices tagged with your NAICS code are a chance to tell the contracting officer that HUBZone firms exist. That matters because a HUBZone set-aside needs a reasonable expectation of two or more HUBZone offers (FAR 19.1305). Our sources sought response template shows how to answer one.

Example (illustrative): say a janitorial firm finds a HUBZone set-aside solicitation in its state. Before bidding, it re-runs the map on its office and staff addresses (bid-day eligibility), checks the size standard, and confirms its SAM.gov registration is active. Only then does it start the proposal.

Pitfall: HUBZone Sole Source (HZS) notices are usually announcements of an award to a specific firm, not open calls for bids. Read the notice type before you spend time on one.

Next steps

You can do the first check today in under an hour, and everything below except paid advisers is free.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Run your office address and every employee's home address on the SBA HUBZone map. Record the type and any expiration date, and work out your residency share against 35%.
  2. Open the SAM.gov HUBZone set-aside search, add your NAICS code, and count active solicitations.
  3. If you're already certified, log in to MySBA Certifications and note your three-year anniversary, so you know when the 90-day recertification window opens.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators. Free counseling funded by the Department of Defense. Counselors can walk you through HUBZone eligibility and your application (APEX Accelerators; DLA HUBZone overview). Good for first-time applicants and firms on a budget. Less suited to complex ownership questions or disputes, and appointment wait times vary by office.
  • SBA certification itself has no application fee (as of October 2026; check the official page), so nobody needs to pay just to apply.
  • Government contracts attorneys or private consultants. Useful if your eligibility depends on edge cases such as legacy employees, an office move, or a protest. They charge their own rates, so get a written quote first. This is usually more than a simple single-office firm needs.

FAQ

What is a HUBZone map used for?

It checks whether a specific address or GPS point lies in a HUBZone and which designation type applies. Businesses use it for their principal office and employee residences, since the program requires both. It doesn't certify a business. That happens through MySBA Certifications.

Is the HUBZone map on sba.gov official?

Yes. The official tool is at maps.certify.sba.gov/hubzone/map, run by SBA as part of its certification platform. Third-party copies may lag behind SBA's data, especially after the July 1, 2026 expirations, so use SBA's map for any decision.

What does it mean if my address shows as HUBZone eligible?

It means that location currently meets one HUBZone designation. Check the type: Census Tract and County results last until the July 2028 update, while Redesignated, Disaster and Governor-designated areas can expire. You still need 35% HUBZone-resident employees, small size, eligible ownership and SBA certification.

How often does the HUBZone map update?

SBA updates census tracts and non-metro counties every five years. The current map took effect in July 2023 and the next update is July 2028. Redesignated, Disaster and Governor-designated areas can be added or expire between those updates, so check again before each HUBZone bid.

What is a HUBZone set-aside contract?

It's a federal contract competition limited to certified HUBZone small businesses, used when a contracting officer expects offers from at least two of them at a fair market price (FAR 19.1305). On SAM.gov these notices carry the code HZC. You must be eligible on the date you submit your offer.

item.title: Small Business Set Aside 51 Rule: 2026 Pass/Fail Checklist
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: The small business set aside 51 rule is really two rules: 51% ownership/control and the 50% limit on subcontracting. See both, plus a 2026 checklist.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

People who search for the "small business set aside 51 rule" are usually mixing up two separate rules. The first is the requirement that at least 51% of a company be unconditionally owned and controlled by qualifying people. It applies to the socioeconomic programs: SDVOSB, VOSB, WOSB, 8(a) and HUBZone (13 CFR 128.202). The second is the limitation on subcontracting in FAR 52.219-14. Under that rule, a prime on a services or supplies set-aside may pay no more than 50% of what the government pays it to subcontractors that aren't "similarly situated." For general construction the cap is 85%, and for special trade construction it is 75%. A plain small business set-aside doesn't test ownership at all. It asks whether you are a small, for-profit U.S. business concern under your NAICS size standard (13 CFR 121.105).

Which option is right for you?

Start with whichever of the two rules is most likely to knock you out in your situation.

Your situationWhat to check firstFirst page to open
First-time bidder, no certificationsWhether you're small under the solicitation's NAICS code. The 51% ownership test doesn't apply to you.SBA size standards, then /sba-size-standards-by-naics-2026-table-steps-appeals/
Veteran or service-disabled veteran ownerVetCert status, because SDVOSB/VOSB credit requires SBA certificationSBA veteran contracting programs
Already winning set-asides (day-to-day work)Your running subcontracting percentage for each base term or option period, since penalties start at $500,000FAR 52.219-14
Construction firmWhether the work is general or special trade (85% vs. 75% cap), and whether materials are excluded13 CFR 125.6
Tight budget, no outside helpFree counseling from an APEX Accelerator before you pay for anythingAPEX Accelerators

What Is a Small Business Set-Aside?

A small business set-aside is a federal contract that only small businesses may compete for. The contracting officer reserves it under FAR Part 19 after market research shows that at least two capable small firms are likely to bid. In the revised FAR Part 19 (the FAR Overhaul deviation text), that "rule of two" sits at 19.104-1(a). It requires a set-aside above the micro-purchase threshold when there is "a reasonable expectation of obtaining offers from two or more responsible small business concerns" that are "competitive in terms of fair market prices, quality, and delivery" (FAR Overhaul Part 19).

The dollar thresholds matter here. As of October 1, 2025, inflation adjustments raised the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) from $250,000 to $350,000 and the micro-purchase threshold from $10,000 to $15,000 (Pillsbury summary of the FAR Council rule). Purchases between those two numbers are reserved for small business when two or more small firms can do the work.

To bid on a set-aside, you need to be all of the following:

  • A business concern. Under 13 CFR 121.105, that means "organized for profit, with a place of business located in the United States," and operating mainly in the U.S. or contributing to the U.S. economy.
  • Small under the size standard for the NAICS code in the solicitation, counting your affiliates (SBA size standards).
  • Registered in SAM.gov with current representations. The steps are in /sam-gov-registration-guide-7-steps-from-uei-to-active/.

A set-aside can cover the whole requirement or only part of it. The differences are in /total-vs-partial-small-business-set-aside-2026-checklist/.

Pitfall: a lot of owners assume they need to be "51% American-owned" or "51% owned by the founder" to qualify for a plain small business set-aside. That isn't in 121.105. The only percentage in that definition is a limit on joint ventures: "no more than 49 percent participation by foreign business entities." The 51% ownership figure comes from the certification programs covered below.

51% Ownership and Control Rule vs. 50% Limitation on Subcontracting: What's the Difference?

The 51% rule decides who has to own and run your company to claim a socioeconomic status. The 50% rule (FAR 52.219-14 / 13 CFR 125.6) caps how much of the contract money you can pass to other firms after award. They apply at different stages and test different things.

51% ownership and controlLimitation on subcontracting
What it testsWho owns and controls your companyWhere the contract dollars go
When it's testedAt application/certification and at offer (status protests)During performance, by the end of the base term and each option period
Main sources13 CFR 128.202–128.203 (VOSB/SDVOSB), 13 CFR 127 (WOSB), 13 CFR 124 (8(a)), 13 CFR 126 (HUBZone)FAR 52.219-14, 13 CFR 125.6
Applies to plain small business set-asides?NoYes, above the SAT
Applies to 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB, WOSB awards?YesYes, at any dollar value (13 CFR 125.6)
The numbersAt least 51% owned and controlled by qualifying individualsServices 50%, supplies 50% (excluding materials), general construction 85%, special trade 75%
Result of failingIneligible for that status; can lose the award through a status protestFine of the greater of $500,000 or the excess subcontracted amount (13 CFR 125.6)

Here is the easy way to keep them apart. The 51% test looks at your cap table and org chart. The subcontracting test looks at your invoices. A company can be 100% owned by a service-disabled veteran and still break the subcontracting rule by sending 70% of a services contract to a large subcontractor. In the other direction, a plain small business that is 0% veteran-owned can comply perfectly with 52.219-14.

One more reason the two get blurred is that the subcontracting rule used to be measured differently. Older versions of FAR 52.219-14 tested the "cost of contract performance incurred for personnel." A FAR rule published January 17, 2024 switched the clause to SBA's "amount paid" approach (Federal Register, FAR: Limitations on Subcontracting Revisions). Some older blog posts still describe the personnel-cost method, so check the date on anything you read.

How Does the 51% Ownership and Control Requirement Work?

At least 51% of the business must be unconditionally and directly owned by one or more qualifying individuals. Those same people must also control management and daily operations. The details differ somewhat by program.

ProgramWho must own 51%+Regulation
SDVOSBOne or more service-disabled veterans13 CFR 128.202
VOSBOne or more veterans13 CFR 128.202
WOSB / EDWOSBOne or more women who are U.S. citizens13 CFR 127.201
8(a)One or more socially and economically disadvantaged individuals13 CFR 124.105
HUBZoneU.S. citizens (or certain entity owners such as tribes and ANCs)13 CFR 126.200

Using the VetCert rules as the model, these are the conditions that most often trip people up:

  1. Direct ownership. The qualifying veteran must hold the 51% "directly, and not through another business entity or trust (including an ESOP)." The one exception is a revocable living trust where the veteran is grantor, trustee and current beneficiary (13 CFR 128.202).
  2. Unconditional ownership. Unexercised stock options, convertible debt and similar rights held by non-veterans "will be treated as exercised" (13 CFR 128.202). If an investor's option would push the veteran below 51% once exercised, the firm fails today.
  3. Highest officer. "A qualifying veteran must hold the highest officer position in the concern (usually President or Chief Executive Officer)" (13 CFR 128.203).
  4. Full-time devotion. The qualifying veteran "generally must devote full time to the business concern during its normal hours of operations" (13 CFR 128.203).
  5. No outside veto over ordinary business. Minority owners may hold veto rights over extraordinary actions such as adding equity holders, dissolution, selling substantially all assets, mergers and bankruptcy (13 CFR 128.203). A minority veto over hiring, budgets or bidding decisions is a red flag.
  6. Economic independence. Non-qualifying individuals can't create relationships so dependent that "the qualifying veteran cannot exercise independent business judgment without great economic risk" (13 CFR 128.203). Lopsided loans or a single landlord-supplier-customer arrangement can cause this.

Example (illustrative): a disabled veteran owns 55% of an LLC, and a non-veteran partner owns 45%. The operating agreement says that "all decisions require unanimous consent of the members." Ownership passes, but control fails, because the 45% partner can block ordinary decisions. Rewriting the operating agreement so that unanimous consent covers only the extraordinary actions listed in 128.203 is the usual fix. Have counsel review it.

The 51% rule doesn't replace the size test. A certified SDVOSB still has to be small under the NAICS code of each solicitation. For the program-specific versions of these checks, see /sdvosb-set-aside-requirements-2026-eligibility-checklist/ and /wosb-certification-requirements-2026-checklist-and-fees/.

How Does the 50% Limitation on Subcontracting (Self-Performance) Rule Work?

The prime must keep a minimum share of the contract dollars in-house, or with similarly situated subcontractors. That share is measured against the amount the government pays the prime. It has nothing to do with ownership percentages.

The percentages, quoted from FAR 52.219-14 as of October 2026:

Contract typeMax paid to non-similarly-situated subsMaterials excluded?Example base and cap (illustrative)
Services (except construction)50% of amount paid by the GovernmentNo$1,000,000 paid → max $500,000 to non-SSE subs
Supplies50% of amount paid, excluding cost of materialsYes$800,000 paid − $300,000 materials = $500,000 base → max $250,000
General construction85% of amount paid, excluding cost of materialsYes$2,000,000 − $600,000 materials = $1,400,000 → max $1,190,000
Special trade construction75% of amount paid, excluding cost of materialsYes$500,000 − $100,000 materials = $400,000 → max $300,000

Four mechanics decide whether you pass.

Similarly situated entities don't count against you. A first-tier subcontractor counts as similarly situated when it has the same small business program status as the prime and is small under the prime contract's NAICS code (FAR 52.219-14). On an SDVOSB set-aside, work you give another small, certified SDVOSB is treated like your own. The subcontractor has to perform with its own employees, and the exclusion ends if it loses its status (13 CFR 125.6).

Timing. Compliance is measured "by the end of the base term of the contract and then by the end of each subsequent option period," or by the end of the performance period for orders (FAR 52.219-14). Being at 60% subcontracted in month three isn't a violation yet. Ending the base year there is.

Scope. Under 13 CFR 125.6, the rule applies to small business set-asides above the SAT and to 8(a), SDVOSB, VOSB, HUBZone and WOSB/EDWOSB awards. The revised FAR Part 19 still prescribes 52.219-14 at 19.104-3(c) and points to it throughout the socioeconomic program sections (FAR Overhaul Part 19).

Supplies have a second rule. If you supply a product you didn't manufacture, the nonmanufacturer rule (clause 52.219-33, prescribed at 19.104-3(e)) applies alongside the subcontracting limit (FAR Overhaul Part 19).

Penalty. A violation carries a fine of "the greater of $500,000 or the dollar amount spent, in excess of permitted levels, by the entity on subcontractors" (13 CFR 125.6).

What's next: the FAR open-case list shows FAR Case 2021-020 (Limitations on Subcontracting) on hold pending further SBA rulemaking. Trade press reports that SBA plans to tighten the construction rules by April 1, 2027 (FedLift). Until a final rule appears in the Federal Register, the percentages above are the ones that apply.

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • Counting 1099 workers as your own staff. SBA generally treats work done by independent contractors as subcontracted. If you rely on them, model them as subcontractor dollars in your tracker (13 CFR 125.6).
  • Checking only at closeout. Track the ratio monthly so you can move work in-house before the base term ends.
  • Assuming a teammate is similarly situated because it's small. It also needs the same status. A small but non-SDVOSB sub on an SDVOSB set-aside counts against your cap.

Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business (SDVOSB) Set-Aside Rules

SDVOSB set-asides require 51% unconditional ownership and control by one or more service-disabled veterans, certified through SBA's VetCert program, plus compliance with the limitation on subcontracting.

VA's Center for Verification and Evaluation (CVE) no longer does this job. Certification moved to SBA on January 1, 2023. Self-certified SDVOSBs got a grace period: firms that applied before January 1, 2024 could keep relying on self-certification for non-VA SDVOSB set-asides until SBA decided their application (Federal Register final rule, Nov. 29, 2022; Maynard Nexsen). VA set-asides never had a grace period. SBA also states that as of December 22, 2024, veteran firms that want subcontracting and goaling credit must hold VetCert certification (SBA).

To get certified:

  1. Confirm your VA service-connected disability rating letter is on hand. SBA requires owners "rated as service-disabled by the VA" (SBA).
  2. Make sure your SAM.gov registration is active, with the same legal name, UEI and address you'll use in the application.
  3. Go to certifications.sba.gov, sign in, and start the Veteran Small Business Certification application (SBA).
  4. Upload ownership documents (operating agreement or bylaws, stock ledger, any trust documents) and control documents (officer list, meeting minutes, resumes).
  5. Before you submit, check every document against the 128.202/128.203 points above: options treated as exercised, the veteran as highest officer, and no ordinary-course veto held by others.
  6. Once you're certified, confirm your status appears in SBA's public search and that your SAM.gov representations match.

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • A minority owner with a broad veto. Narrow it to the extraordinary actions listed in 13 CFR 128.203.
  • A veteran who also holds a full-time outside job. This can fail the full-time devotion test. Document the hours, or restructure before you apply.
  • Teaming with a non-SDVOSB firm that does most of the work. This can fail 52.219-14. It can also trigger the ostensible subcontractor rule, which treats the prime and sub as affiliates (13 CFR 121.103).

Veteran-Owned Small Business (VOSB) Set-Aside Rules

Set-asides for veteran-owned firms whose owners aren't service-disabled exist mainly at the Department of Veterans Affairs, under its Veterans First program. The 51% veteran ownership and control test still applies, and the firm must be SBA-certified.

Outside VA, there's no governmentwide VOSB set-aside. SBA's own summary says "Certified VOSBs may also compete for sole-source and set-aside contracts from the VA," while SDVOSBs compete "across the federal government" (SBA).

At VA, the order is fixed by statute (38 U.S.C. 8127–8128) and by VA's acquisition regulation. The contracting officer considers SDVOSB set-asides first, then VOSB set-asides. If no acceptable SDVOSB offers arrive, the set-aside is withdrawn and may be re-set-aside for VOSBs (VAAR Subpart 819.70).

What to do as a VOSB owner:

  1. Get VetCert certification as a VOSB at certifications.sba.gov. The ownership test is the same 51% "one or more veterans" standard (13 CFR 128.202).
  2. On SAM.gov Contract Opportunities, filter by the Set Aside option for veteran-owned small business and by VA as the department.
  3. Read each VA solicitation to see whether it's SDVOSB-only or open to VOSBs. A VOSB can't bid on an SDVOSB-only set-aside.
  4. Plan your subcontracting the same way an SDVOSB would. The limitation on subcontracting covers VOSB awards too (13 CFR 125.6).

Example (illustrative): a veteran-owned janitorial firm without a disability rating sees a VA facilities-services solicitation marked SDVOSB. It can't bid as the prime. Its options are to subcontract to an SDVOSB prime (counting against that prime's 50% cap) or to watch for the same requirement if VA withdraws the SDVOSB set-aside and re-competes it for VOSBs.

Pass/Fail Compliance Checklist for 2026 Set-Aside Bids

Check the two thresholds separately before you bid. First confirm your size and any 51% ownership/control status. Then work out whether your planned subcontracting stays within the self-performance limit for that contract type.

Part A: eligibility at the time of offer

#CheckPass ifSource
1SAM.gov registrationStatus is Active through the award dateSAM.gov
2Size under the solicitation's NAICSUnder the size standard, including all affiliatesSBA size standards
3Size measurement methodReceipts averaged over the correct period, or employees averaged over the correct period13 CFR 121.104, 121.106
4Status certification (if the set-aside requires one)Certified, and the certification appears in SBA's public searchSBA
551% direct, unconditional ownershipQualifying owners hold ≥51% with all options treated as exercised13 CFR 128.202
6ControlQualifying owner is the highest officer, full time, with no ordinary-course veto held by others13 CFR 128.203

Part B: performance plan

#CheckPass ifSource
7Contract type identifiedYou know whether it's services, supplies, general construction or special tradeFAR 52.219-14
8Planned non-SSE subcontract dollars≤50% / 50% net of materials / 85% / 75% of the baseFAR 52.219-14
9Each teammate's status verifiedEvery sub you count as similarly situated has the same status and is small under your NAICSFAR 52.219-14
10Primary and vital workYour own staff performs the core work, not a large sub13 CFR 121.103
11Nonmanufacturer rule (supplies)You manufacture the item or qualify under 52.219-33FAR Overhaul Part 19
12Tracking set upA monthly ledger of amounts paid to SSE and non-SSE subs, by base term and option period13 CFR 125.6

A single "fail" in Part A means you shouldn't bid as the prime yet. A fail in Part B usually means restructuring the team, not walking away. Bring more labor in-house, swap a large sub for a similarly situated one, or bid as a sub to another prime.

How to run the numbers for check 8 (illustrative, services):

  1. Estimate the total you expect the government to pay you for the base year. Example: $600,000.
  2. List each subcontractor's expected payments and mark each one SSE or non-SSE.
  3. Add up the non-SSE amounts. Example: $250,000 to a large IT firm and $40,000 to independent contractors comes to $290,000.
  4. Divide by the total: $290,000 ÷ $600,000 = 48.3%. That passes, but only barely, so watch it monthly.

For the bid itself, including pricing and what to submit, see /how-to-bid-on-government-contracts-7-steps-2026-costs/.

Common Mistakes That Trigger a Small Business Set-Aside Protest

Most size and status protests come from four mistakes:

  • confusing the two "51%" figures
  • miscounting affiliates' revenue or employees
  • leaning on a large subcontractor for the core work
  • going over the subcontracting limit without tracking it

Size is judged as of a fixed date: generally the date you submit your initial offer that includes price (13 CFR 121.404). Competitors can file a size protest within a short window after the apparent awardee is named. For negotiated procurements, that window is generally five business days (13 CFR 121.1004). That leaves you very little time to fix paperwork, so get it right before you bid.

Mistake 1: believing ownership is the only test. For example, an owner reads "51% owned and controlled" and assumes a plain small business set-aside requires it. Meanwhile the firm is too big once a sister company's receipts are counted. Fix: run the affiliation analysis under 13 CFR 121.103. Common ownership, common management, identity of interest (such as close family members in similar businesses) and negative control can all create affiliation.

Mistake 2: the ostensible subcontractor problem. If your subcontractor performs the "primary and vital" requirements, or you depend on it unusually, SBA can treat the two of you as joint venturers and combine your sizes (13 CFR 121.103). This often happens alongside a breach of 52.219-14, but it's a separate size issue that can cost you the award before performance even starts.

Mistake 3: using the wrong measurement period. Receipts-based standards use an average over the prior completed fiscal years set out in 13 CFR 121.104. Employee-based standards use the average over the period in 13 CFR 121.106. Pick the wrong period and a firm near the line can flip from small to other-than-small.

Mistake 4: status drift after certification. You sell 10% of the company to an investor with a conversion right, or the qualifying owner takes a full-time job elsewhere. Your certification may still look valid, but the 128.202/128.203 tests may no longer be met. Fix: re-run Part A of the checklist whenever ownership, officers or bylaws change.

Mistake 5: no subcontracting ledger. The rule is measured cumulatively at the end of each base term or option period (FAR 52.219-14), so a firm with no running tally finds out too late. Fix: a monthly spreadsheet with columns for invoice amount, payee, SSE yes/no and cumulative percentage.

If you've lost a size determination, the appeals process is covered in /sba-size-standards-by-naics-2026-table-steps-appeals/.

Next steps

You can do the core of this today without outside help. If your structure is complicated, there are free and paid ways to get it reviewed.

DIY today:

  1. Open your SAM.gov entity record and confirm your NAICS codes and size representations. Then check the size standard for the NAICS code in the next solicitation you plan to bid on.
  2. If you claim (or want to claim) SDVOSB, VOSB, WOSB, 8(a) or HUBZone status, read your operating agreement or bylaws against the six ownership and control conditions above. Mark every veto, option and trust.
  3. For your current or next bid, fill in Part B of the checklist with real numbers. Write down which subs you're treating as similarly situated, and why.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) provide counseling on registration, certification and bid preparation through DoD-funded local centers (APEX Accelerators). They suit first-time bidders and owners on a budget. They aren't the right choice for a legal opinion on a disputed ownership structure or a pending protest, because they don't act as your attorney, and wait times depend on the local center.
  • A government contracts attorney is the better fit if you have convertible notes, trusts, a minority veto, a joint venture or an active size/status protest. Fees are usually hourly and vary widely by firm and region, so ask for an engagement estimate up front (as of October 2026; check with the firm). This is overkill for a simple single-owner LLC bidding its first services set-aside.

Related guides on this site:

  • /sdvosb-set-aside-requirements-2026-eligibility-checklist/
  • /8-a-certification-requirements-2026-pass-fail-checklist/
  • /hubzone-map-2026-address-check-steps-and-expiry-dates/
  • /sources-sought-notice-5-step-response-template-2026/ (use a sources sought response to help the agency see enough small firms to meet the rule of two)

FAQ

What is a small business set aside?

It's a federal contract that only small businesses may compete for. The contracting officer reserves it when market research shows a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses at fair market prices (FAR Overhaul Part 19, 19.104-1(a)). Purchases between $15,000 and $350,000 are generally reserved for small businesses when that test is met.

What is the 51% rule for small business?

The term usually refers to the requirement that one or more qualifying individuals (service-disabled veterans, veterans, women, or disadvantaged individuals) unconditionally own at least 51% of the company and control it. That's what it takes to claim SDVOSB, VOSB, WOSB or 8(a) status (13 CFR 128.202). It doesn't apply to plain small business set-asides. It's also separate from the 50% limitation on subcontracting.

How is the limitation on subcontracting percentage calculated?

Divide the amount you paid to subcontractors that aren't similarly situated by the amount the government paid you. For supplies and construction, subtract the cost of materials from both figures first. The result must stay at or below 50% (services and supplies), 85% (general construction) or 75% (special trade). It's measured at the end of the base term and each option period (FAR 52.219-14).

Who certifies SDVOSB status now that VA CVE is gone?

The U.S. Small Business Administration does, through its Veteran Small Business Certification (VetCert) program at certifications.sba.gov. SBA took over from VA's CVE on January 1, 2023 (Federal Register). Certification is required for VA set-asides and for SDVOSB credit governmentwide (SBA).

Can a veteran-owned business bid on SDVOSB set-asides without being service-disabled?

No, not as the prime. SDVOSB set-asides require 51% ownership and control by veterans with a VA service-connected disability rating (13 CFR 128.202). A certified VOSB can compete for VA's VOSB set-asides, which VA uses after SDVOSB set-asides (VAAR 819.70). It can also work as a subcontractor to an SDVOSB prime.
