item.title: How to Bid on Government Contracts: 7 Steps, 2026 Costs
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How to bid on government contracts in 2026: register free in SAM.gov, find set-asides, and submit a compliant bid, with state portal fees and official links.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To bid on government contracts, first register your business for free in SAM.gov. That gives you a Unique Entity ID (UEI) and a CAGE code. Next, look up the NAICS codes and size standards that fit your work. Then search SAM.gov Contract Opportunities for notices you can win, and send exactly what the solicitation asks for before the deadline. Many first awards go to small businesses through set-asides, so check whether you qualify for an SBA certification before you start chasing larger contracts.

Which option is right for you?

Where you should start depends on what's stopping you right now, so pick the row that fits.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner with no registrations yetFull SAM.gov entity registration ("All Awards")SAM.gov Entity Registration
Already registered, want work this monthSmall-dollar notices and set-asides in your NAICS codeSAM.gov Contract Opportunities search
Owner is a woman, veteran, or in a HUBZoneSBA certification (free)MySBA Certifications
Tight budget, want guidanceA local APEX Accelerator (free or nominal cost)APEX Accelerators
You sell mostly to one stateThat state's vendor portalMyFloridaMarketPlace, Cal eProcure, or Texas CMBL (table below)
You already hold a GSA ScheduleGSA eBuy RFQs under your SINsGSA: Research active solicitations

Why each row: SAM.gov registration comes before anything else on the federal side. Set-asides reduce your competition. SBA certifications cost nothing to apply for. APEX counselors are free or nominal-cost. And state portals run separately from SAM.gov.

How to Register to Bid on Government Contracts

To register, get a UEI, finish a full SAM.gov entity registration, and list NAICS codes that match your services. All of it is free.

SAM.gov describes four phases: review your options, create a SAM.gov account through Login.gov, gather your information, and submit. You also have to pick between two outcomes. With a UEI only, you can do limited things like sub-award reporting, but you can't pursue federal awards. To bid on prime contracts you need full registration. Getting a UEI, registering, and keeping the registration active all cost nothing, according to GSA and the SAM.gov Entity Registration Checklist.

Registration steps with the on-screen labels

  1. Go to SAM.gov and select Sign In. Create or link a Login.gov account with multi-factor authentication.
  2. Open your Workspace. In the Entity section, select Get Started, then Register Entity.
  3. When it asks about the purpose of registration, choose All Awards (not "Financial Assistance Awards Only"). Only the first option lets you bid on contracts.
  4. Enter your legal business name and physical address exactly as the IRS has them. This creates your UEI.
  5. Fill in the core data: TIN, EFT banking details, NAICS codes, PSC codes, and points of contact. All of these are on the checklist.
  6. Complete Representations and Certifications. This is where you state your size and socio-economic status for each NAICS code.
  7. Submit. The checklist notes that IRS TIN validation alone takes several days. A CAGE code is assigned as part of the process, and you may be asked for a notarized letter.

For the screen-by-screen version, see our SAM.gov registration guide: 7 steps from UEI to active.

Common registration mistakes and fixes

  • Name mismatch with the IRS. "Smith Electric LLC" and "Smith Electric, L.L.C." can fail validation. Fix: copy the name character for character from your IRS EIN letter.
  • Paying a "registration service." Third parties sometimes send official-looking emails offering paid SAM help. Fix: SAM.gov is free. Real support comes from the Federal Service Desk at fsd.gov, which GSA lists as the official help resource.
  • Letting it lapse. Registrations expire. SAM.gov says you must renew every 365 days. Fix: put a reminder on your calendar 60 days before your expiration date.
  • Only one NAICS code. Agencies search by NAICS. Fix: list every code you can actually perform, and check the size standard for each in our SBA size standards by NAICS table.

What Is Needed to Bid on Government Contracts

To bid you need an active SAM.gov registration, a UEI and CAGE code, any certifications the notice requires, and a response that meets its technical and pricing terms.

Registration only lets you in. The solicitation decides everything else. Here's what a typical bid packet contains:

ItemWhere it comes fromRequired when
Active SAM.gov registration (UEI + CAGE)SAM.govNearly all federal prime contracts
Correct NAICS code and size statusYour SAM reps and certsAny small business set-aside
SBA certification (8(a), WOSB/EDWOSB, HUBZone, VetCert SDVOSB)MySBA CertificationsSet-asides reserved for that program
Technical response / capability narrativeYouRFPs, and many RFQs
Price or quote (often a pricing sheet the agency provides)YouEvery solicitation
Past performance referencesYour prior customers (public or private)Most best-value RFPs
Signed forms (e.g., SF 1449, SF 33, amendments)The solicitation packageWhen the notice says so
BondsA surety companyMany construction contracts

Example: a small janitorial RFQ

Say a VA medical center posts a total small business set-aside RFQ for janitorial services under NAICS 561720 (this is an illustration, not a real notice). A complete quote would include the signed SF 1449, every acknowledged amendment, the completed price schedule, a short technical approach, and the past performance references the RFQ asks for. You'd also need an active SAM.gov registration where your size for 561720 is "small." If any of those pieces is missing, the quote can be rejected before anyone looks at your price.

Before you have a live notice to answer, write a one-page capability statement. Agencies and primes ask for it during market research. Our capability statement example shows the five sections buyers read first.

What Is Bidding on Government Contracts

Bidding on government contracts means submitting a formal offer, called a quote, proposal, or sealed bid, in response to a government solicitation that states the requirements and the evaluation method.

The kind of solicitation sets how you respond. The FAR uses three main formats:

  • RFQ (Request for Quotation). Common for simplified acquisitions. A quote is not a binding offer. The government's order creates the contract.
  • RFP (Request for Proposals). Used for negotiated procurements under FAR Part 15. It's evaluated on factors such as technical approach, past performance, and price, and the agency can trade them off against each other.
  • IFB (Invitation for Bids). Sealed bidding under FAR Part 14. Award goes to the lowest-priced responsive, responsible bidder.

Federal agencies post contract actions over $25,000 on SAM.gov, per the SBA. Smaller buys can happen without a public notice. Notices also come in stages. A Sources Sought or RFI is market research and not yet a solicitation. A Presolicitation gives advance notice. A Solicitation or Combined Synopsis/Solicitation is where you actually bid.

For example, a "Combined Synopsis/Solicitation" for office furniture under $350,000 is typically an RFQ. You'd answer it with a priced quote and the listed forms, not a 50-page proposal. Our guide to RFQ vs RFP: 5 FAR clues shows how to tell the two apart from the notice text.

What Does Bidding on Government Contracts Mean

Government bidding isn't an auction. You compete on compliance, qualifications, and price against criteria written into the solicitation, and the lowest number doesn't always win.

Only sealed bidding under FAR Part 14 comes close to "lowest price wins," and even then the bid has to be responsive and the bidder responsible. Under FAR Part 15, the agency may use a best-value tradeoff and pay more for a stronger technical approach. It may also use "lowest price technically acceptable," where you have to pass every technical factor before price counts at all.

Pitfalls that cost first-time bidders the award

  • Missing the deadline by minutes. Late offers are generally rejected. Fix: submit at least 24 hours early, and confirm the time zone listed in the notice.
  • Ignoring amendments. Agencies change requirements through amendments posted to the same notice. Fix: before you submit, reopen the notice, look at the Attachments/Links section, and acknowledge every amendment the way the notice says to.
  • Not following the format. Page limits, font size, and file naming rules are often enforced. Fix: build a compliance checklist from the instructions to offerors (Section L in many RFPs, or the "Instructions" paragraph in RFQs) and the evaluation criteria (Section M).
  • Underpricing to "buy" the contract. In many evaluations an unrealistically low price can be marked as risk. Fix: price from real labor, materials, and overhead.

What Is the Website to Bid on Government Contracts

SAM.gov is the main federal website for finding and answering contract opportunities. GSA Schedule holders also get RFQs through GSA eBuy, and some agencies use their own portals.

How you submit depends on the notice. Some say to email the contracting officer, some say to upload through SAM.gov, and some point to an agency system. Whatever the "Contact Information" and instructions sections say is the rule. If you hold a GSA Multiple Award Schedule, GSA explains that eBuy RFQs are visible only to contract holders in the matching Special Item Numbers (SINs). That's the main limitation of eBuy: if you don't have a Schedule, you won't see those RFQs at all.

How to find a bid you can win on SAM.gov

  1. Go to SAM.gov, open Search, and select the Contract Opportunities domain.
  2. In the keyword box, enter your primary NAICS code (example: 238210 for electrical contractors).
  3. Under Status, keep Active selected.
  4. Under Notice Type, check Solicitation and Combined Synopsis/Solicitation for bids you can submit now. Add Sources Sought and Presolicitation to see what's coming.
  5. Under Set Aside, select Total Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.5) or your certification type.
  6. Under Place of Performance, enter your state so you only see jobs you can staff.
  7. Sort by Response Date and save the search while you're signed in.

Sources Sought notices are often where small businesses can shape whether a contract gets set aside at all. Our 5-step sources sought response template covers what to send.

Two other free federal tools are useful. USASpending.gov shows who won earlier versions of a contract and at what price. SBA's SubNet lists subcontracting opportunities from large prime contractors, which is a realistic first step if you have no federal past performance yet.

The 7 Steps From SAM.gov to a Submitted Bid

Here is the full sequence in order. Each step depends on the one before it.

  1. Confirm your size. Find your NAICS codes and check your revenue or employee count against SBA's size standard for each. → SBA size standards
  2. Register in SAM.gov ("All Awards"). Allow time for IRS TIN validation. → SAM.gov Entity Registration
  3. Apply for any SBA certification you qualify for. It's free, and you can apply for up to four at once. → SBA certifications
  4. Build a capability statement and fill out your SBS profile. Agencies search the Small Business Search database, which is filled in from your SAM data. → SBA: How to win contracts
  5. Search SAM.gov daily and shortlist notices. Bid only where you meet the requirements, can perform at the place of performance, and can price competitively.
  6. Build a compliance matrix and write the response. List every "shall," "must," required form, and amendment, then answer each one in the order the notice uses.
  7. Submit early, then confirm receipt. Use the exact method the notice names. Keep the email timestamp or upload confirmation.

A bid/no-bid rule helps here. For example, you might pass on any notice where you can't name a similar past project, or where the response window is shorter than the time you need to get subcontractor quotes. Pick a rule that matches how big your team is.

How Much Does It Cost to Bid on Government Contracts

Registering in SAM.gov and applying for SBA certifications both cost nothing. What you actually spend is time, plus bonds for some construction work and any optional consultants or state fees.

Cost itemOfficial price (as of October 2026; check the official page)Source
UEI + SAM.gov registration + annual renewal$0GSA
SBA certifications (8(a), WOSB, HUBZone, VetCert)$0 to applySBA
APEX Accelerator counselingFree or nominalSBA
Texas CMBL registration$70 per yearTexas Comptroller
MyFloridaMarketPlace registration$0, plus a transaction fee on payments (0.7% currently)Florida DMS
Cal eProcure registration and SB/DVBE certification$0California DGS
Proposal preparationYour staff time; varies by solicitationn/a
Surety bonds (construction)Set by the surety, based on your credit and the jobn/a

Federal dollar thresholds affect how much paperwork a contract involves. On October 1, 2025, the FAR's inflation adjustment raised the micro-purchase threshold from $10,000 to $15,000 and the simplified acquisition threshold (SAT) from $250,000 to $350,000 (Centre Law Group summary; Pillsbury). Buys under the SAT use simplified procedures, which usually means shorter quotes. That's why they make a good first target.

Pitfall: the SBA's own "how to win contracts" page still says set-asides apply automatically to most contracts under $150,000, which is an older threshold. Go by the current FAR numbers and by what the notice itself says about set-asides.

How to Bid on Government Contracts as a Small Business

Small businesses can bid on set-aside contracts reserved for small firms. SBA certifications (8(a), HUBZone, WOSB, SDVOSB) open up even smaller pools that large companies can't enter.

The government's goal is to award 23% of federal contract dollars to small businesses. Separate goals cover women-owned small businesses (5%), service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses (5%), and HUBZone firms (3%), per the SBA's goaling page. The "rule of two" survived the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul. When contracting officers reasonably expect offers from two or more responsible small businesses at fair market prices, they still have to set the buy aside. One change: for task and delivery orders under multiple-award contracts, set-asides are now discretionary (SmallGovCon; PilieroMazza). As of mid-2026, agencies are using the new Part 19 text through class deviations, and formal Part 19 rulemaking hasn't been published yet. Check the clause list in each solicitation.

ProgramCore eligibility (summary)Main contracting benefit
Small business (no certification)Under the SBA size standard for the NAICS codeTotal and partial small business set-asides
8(a)51%+ owned by socially and economically disadvantaged U.S. citizens; personal net worth $850,000 or less; 9-year term (SBA 8(a) program)Sole-source awards up to $8.5M (manufacturing) / $5.5M (other) after the October 2025 inflation adjustment (Centre Law Group summary; check the SBA 8(a) program page)
HUBZonePrincipal office in a HUBZone; 35% of employees live in one (SBA HUBZone program)10% price evaluation preference; HUBZone set-asides (SBA HUBZone program)
WOSB / EDWOSB51%+ owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizensSet-asides in eligible NAICS codes (SBA WOSB program)
SDVOSB (VetCert)51%+ owned and controlled by service-disabled veteransSDVOSB set-asides and sole-source awards (SBA veteran contracting programs)

Small business steps

  1. Check that you're small under the NAICS code on the specific notice, not just your primary code.
  2. In MySBA Certifications, select Get Started, then choose the programs you want. You can apply for up to four at once.
  3. While you wait, bid on Total Small Business Set-Aside notices. They don't require a certification.
  4. If you'd be the prime, read the limitations on subcontracting clause. For services, you generally can't pay more than 50% of the amount paid to you to non-similarly-situated subcontractors (SBA).

The 8(a) program doesn't fit everyone. It has net-worth and income caps, requires two years in business in most cases, and has a nine-year limit (SBA 8(a) program). If your firm doesn't meet those, a WOSB or HUBZone certification may fit better. For program-specific checks, see our 8(a) pass/fail checklist, SDVOSB eligibility checklist, and total vs partial set-aside checklist.

How to Bid on Government Contracts by State (Florida, California, Texas)

Each state runs its own procurement portal, separate from SAM.gov, and you have to register there as a vendor too. Being registered in SAM.gov doesn't register you with a state.

StatePortalRegistration cost (as of October 2026; check the official page)Notable rule
FloridaMyFloridaMarketPlace (MFMP); bids posted on the Vendor Bid SystemFreeTransaction fee on payments, currently 0.7% (Florida DMS)
CaliforniaCal eProcure (caleprocure.ca.gov)FreeCertified SB/DVBE firms get a 5% bid preference; goals are 25% SB and 3% DVBE (DGS)
TexasCentralized Master Bidders List (CMBL); bids on ESBD via Texas SmartBuy$70 per yearCMBL is the list agencies use to send bid notices (Texas Comptroller)

State registration steps

  1. Florida: Register at the MFMP vendor site, enter your commodity codes, and then watch the Vendor Bid System for solicitations. Your quote should account for the transaction fee, since it's taken out of payments.
  2. California: On Cal eProcure, select Sell to the State, then Register Now. If you're eligible, apply for SB or DVBE certification through the SB/DVBE page. California SB status requires 100 or fewer employees and average annual gross receipts of $19M or less, with principals living in California (DGS).
  3. Texas: Register in the CMBL, pick NIGP commodity codes, pay the $70 fee, and keep your email address current so bid notices reach you.

One common mistake: California's DVBE program uses its own state rules, which are different from federal SDVOSB rules, so one certification doesn't count for the other. The same goes for Texas HUB and federal HUBZone, which are separate programs. Cities and counties often run their own portals as well. Reddit threads and "how to bid in Guyana, Canada, or the UK" searches lead to entirely different systems. This guide covers only U.S. federal work and these three states.

Next steps

Pick one federal action and one state action you can finish this week.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Open SAM.gov Entity Registration, download the checklist, and put your EIN letter and bank routing details in one folder.
  2. Look up your NAICS size standard and write down every code you qualify for.
  3. Run one SAM.gov Contract Opportunities search with your NAICS code, Active status, and a small business set-aside filter. Save the three notices closest to work you've already done.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • APEX Accelerators (free or nominal cost, per SBA). They suit first-time bidders who want someone to review their registration and their first bids. They're less useful if you need someone to write proposals for you, because counselors advise and don't write your bid.
  • SBA resource partners such as Small Business Development Centers (free counseling directory). These work well for general business and pricing questions, but contracting depth varies by office.
  • Private proposal or registration consultants (fees set by each firm; as of October 2026, no official price exists). They can make sense for complex RFPs if you have budget. Don't hire one for SAM.gov registration itself, because that is free and the Federal Service Desk supports it.

FAQ

How do you register to bid on government contracts?

Create a Login.gov-linked SAM.gov account. Then select Get Started and Register Entity in your Workspace, and choose All Awards. Enter your IRS-matched legal name, TIN, banking, NAICS codes, and reps and certs. Registration is free and has to be renewed every 365 days.

What is needed to bid on government contracts?

You need an active SAM.gov registration with a UEI and CAGE code, and you need to be small under the notice's NAICS code if it's a set-aside. Some notices also require an SBA certification. After that, the solicitation lists the rest: signed forms, acknowledged amendments, a price schedule, and usually a technical response and past performance.

What is the website to bid on government contracts?

For federal work it's SAM.gov, under the Contract Opportunities search. GSA Schedule holders also receive RFQs on GSA eBuy, and only for their awarded SINs. States use their own portals, such as MyFloridaMarketPlace, Cal eProcure, and the Texas CMBL/ESBD.

How much does it cost to bid on government contracts?

SAM.gov registration and SBA certification applications are free. Your main costs are proposal-writing time, bonds for some construction work, and optional consultants. State fees vary: Texas CMBL is $70 a year, and Florida takes a transaction fee (currently 0.7%) from payments (as of October 2026; check the official pages).

item.title: WOSB Certification Requirements: 2026 Checklist and Fees
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: WOSB certification requirements for 2026: 51% ownership and control tests, EDWOSB limits, document mistakes, and free SBA vs. third-party certifier fees.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To meet WOSB certification requirements, your business must be small under SBA's size standard for its primary NAICS code. It must also be at least 51% unconditionally and directly owned and controlled by one or more women who are U.S. citizens, and a woman must run day-to-day operations and make long-term decisions (SBA). You can't self-certify anymore. You get certified either free through SBA's MySBA Certifications portal or through one of four SBA-approved third-party certifiers that charge a fee. Either way, your certification has to show up in MySBA Certifications before you can bid on WOSB set-asides.

Which option is right for you?

For most first-time applicants, the free SBA application is the best place to start. Pay a third-party certifier only if you also want a private-sector WBE certificate or a faster review.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, not yet registered for federal workGet an active SAM.gov registration, then apply free with SBASAM.gov
Registered in SAM, documents in order, no rushFree SBA WOSB application (it costs nothing and covers everything a federal set-aside requires)MySBA Certifications
You also sell to corporations that ask for "WBE" statusWBENC: the WOSB certificate comes free with the WBE applicationWBENC WOSB page
Tight budget but you'd like an outside reviewerU.S. Women's Chamber of Commerce: $275 for members, $350 for non-membersUSWCC WOSB certification
You think you qualify as economically disadvantagedApply for EDWOSB (it includes WOSB) and gather 3 years of personal tax returns firstSBA WOSB program page
A bid is due within weeksNeither path is likely to finish in time, so bid on open small business set-asides insteadTotal vs Partial Small Business Set Aside

What Is WOSB Certification?

WOSB (Women-Owned Small Business) certification is an SBA designation. It lets women-owned businesses compete for the federal contracts set aside under the WOSB Federal Contracting Program. Without it, a contracting officer can't count your firm toward a WOSB set-aside, even if women own 100% of the company.

The program exists to help agencies reach a statutory goal: 5% of federal prime contracting dollars should go to women-owned small businesses (SBA). Agencies often fall short. The Congressional Research Service reports that the 5% prime goal was met in only two of the five years from FY2019 to FY2023, and reached 4.91% in FY2023 (CRS R46322, June 2024). That gap gives contracting officers a reason to look for certified WOSBs.

Certification gives you access to three things:

  • WOSB set-asides. These are competitions limited to certified WOSBs, in NAICS codes where SBA has found women-owned businesses are substantially underrepresented.
  • EDWOSB set-asides. These are limited to economically disadvantaged WOSBs, in industries where women-owned firms are underrepresented.
  • Sole-source awards. Since October 1, 2025, the ceilings are $5.5 million for most contracts and $8.5 million for manufacturing, after the FAR inflation adjustment (Federal Register, Aug. 27, 2025; CRS IF13123).

The industry restriction matters. As of SBA's March 2022 list, 646 of 1,023 six-digit NAICS codes qualified for WOSB set-asides, and another 113 qualified for EDWOSB-only set-asides (CRS R46322). Before you apply, check your primary NAICS code against SBA's current eligible NAICS list. For example, if your code is on neither list, WOSB set-asides in that code won't exist. Certification could still help you in other codes you work in.

SBA WOSB Certification Requirements

To qualify, a business must be at least 51% owned and controlled by one or more women who are U.S. citizens, and it must meet SBA's size standard for its industry. The details in 13 CFR Part 127 are what decide most applications.

RequirementWhat SBA checksRule
Small businessAverage receipts or employees under the size standard for your primary NAICSSBA size standards
CitizenshipEach qualifying woman is a U.S. citizen (passport or birth certificate)SBA
51% ownership, unconditionalNo voting trusts, executory agreements, or restrictions on voting rights13 CFR 127.201
51% ownership, directNot held through another company. A living trust counts only if the woman is grantor, trustee, and sole beneficiary13 CFR 127.201
Every class of interest51% of each class of LLC units or partnership interests, and 51% of each class of voting stock plus 51% of all stock13 CFR 127.201
Economic benefitsWomen get at least 51% of distributions and retained earnings13 CFR 127.201
ControlWomen handle both long-term decisions and day-to-day management13 CFR 127.202
Highest officerA woman holds the top officer position and has the management experience to run the firm13 CFR 127.202
Full timeThat woman generally works full time during normal business hours13 CFR 127.202
Board or managersCorporations: women control the board. LLCs: women are the managing members with control over all decisions13 CFR 127.202
Men's roleMen can't control the firm or have the power to control it, and can't out-earn the highest-ranking woman without a justification13 CFR 127.202

Some points tend to surprise applicants.

You don't need the technical license. The woman in charge doesn't have to hold the electrical license or engineering credential herself. She does have to show "ultimate managerial and supervisory control" over the people who do (13 CFR 127.202).

Community property is ignored. If you live in a community property state, SBA disregards your spouse's community interest when it counts ownership (13 CFR 127.201).

Stock options count against you. Unexercised options held by women are ignored. Options held by men are treated as if they had already been exercised, which can push the women's share below 51% (13 CFR 127.201).

Size is set by NAICS code, not by the program. Check your number before you apply. If you're close to the limit, use the method in SBA Size Standards by NAICS.

EDWOSB Certification Requirements

EDWOSB starts with every WOSB ownership and control rule. On top of that, each qualifying woman owner has to pass three personal financial tests set by SBA. If you're certified as an EDWOSB, you're also eligible for WOSB set-asides.

TestLimitWhat's excludedRule
Personal net worthLess than $850,000Your ownership interest in the business, equity in your primary residence, and funds in an IRA or other official retirement account13 CFR 127.203
Adjusted gross income$400,000 or less, averaged over the previous three yearsS-corp, LLC, or partnership distributions that were reinvested in the business or paid only to cover the taxes on that income13 CFR 127.203
Total assetsFair market value of $6.5 million or lessRetirement accounts13 CFR 127.203

(Limits as of October 2026; check the SBA program page.)

Here's an example with illustrative numbers. Your house has $400,000 in equity, your 60% stake in the company is worth $1.2 million, your 401(k) holds $300,000, and you have $250,000 in brokerage and savings with no other debts. Your counted net worth is about $250,000, which is under the limit. Your total assets for the $6.5 million test, without the retirement account, come to roughly $1.85 million. Both tests pass.

Several things trip up EDWOSB applicants:

  • AGI over $400,000 creates a presumption, and you can rebut it. It doesn't automatically disqualify you. If one year spiked because of a one-time pass-through distribution, you can document why it isn't typical (13 CFR 127.203).
  • Assets you recently gave to family can still count. Transfers to relatives within two years before you apply are counted as yours. The exceptions are payments for education, medical care, and customary gifts for special occasions (13 CFR 127.203).
  • SBA may look at your spouse's finances. This applies if your spouse has a role in the business, has given it financial support, or runs a similar business (13 CFR 127.203).
  • You have to keep qualifying. Certified firms go through a program examination every three years (SBA). If your net worth grows past $850,000, plan on losing EDWOSB status while you keep WOSB.

How to Get WOSB Certification

Get an active SAM.gov registration and gather your ownership and control documents. Then apply free through MySBA Certifications at certifications.sba.gov or through an approved third-party certifier. Both paths end in MySBA Certifications.

Path A: free SBA application

  1. Confirm your NAICS code and size. Check your primary code against the size standard and the WOSB eligible NAICS list.
  2. Activate your SAM.gov registration. You need a Unique Entity ID and an active entity registration. The SAM.gov Registration Guide covers each screen. WBENC warns that SAM validation, normally 3–5 business days, has been taking several weeks because of notarization requirements (WBENC).
  3. Make sure SAM matches your governing documents. The legal name, address, and ownership details should agree with your operating agreement or bylaws, because SBA declines applications when the information is inconsistent (13 CFR Part 127, Subpart C).
  4. Gather the documents listed in the table below.
  5. Sign in at certifications.sba.gov with Login.gov. The Login.gov email should be one you'll still be checking in six months.
  6. Pick the program. Choose WOSB, or EDWOSB if you meet the financial tests. Answer the eligibility questions about ownership, control, and citizenship, and upload your documents.
  7. Submit, then watch for requests. SBA tells you whether your package is complete. If it isn't, it tells you what's missing (13 CFR Part 127, Subpart C). Slow replies stall your file.

Path B: third-party certifier

  1. Do steps 1–3 above.
  2. Apply with one of the four SBA-approved certifiers: El Paso Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, National Women Business Owners Corporation (NWBOC), U.S. Women's Chamber of Commerce (USWCC), or WBENC (SBA).
  3. Complete their review. WBENC, for example, does a document review and then a site-visit interview with the woman owner (WBENC).
  4. Upload your proof of citizenship and the certifier's documentation to MySBA Certifications before you bid (SBA). If you skip this step, contracting officers can't verify your status.

Documents to have ready

Business typeCore documents
AllProof of U.S. citizenship for each qualifying woman. Signed federal personal and business tax returns. Personal and business bank statements. Articles of organization or incorporation. Assumed or fictitious name certificates. Any joint venture agreements (13 CFR Part 127, Subpart C)
LLCOperating agreement and all amendments
CorporationBylaws, stock ledger, stock certificates, board minutes
PartnershipPartnership agreement
EDWOSB applicantsThree years of personal tax returns plus a personal financial statement for each qualifying woman (13 CFR 127.203)

WBENC also asks for a SAM Entity Overview printout and proof of employees, such as four quarters of IRS Form 941, a W-3, or an employee list (WBENC).

Common process mistakes

  • Applying with an expired SAM registration. Fix: renew in SAM first. The registration has to be renewed every year.
  • Uploading unsigned tax returns. SBA's rule asks for signed copies, so re-scan them with signatures.
  • Uploading only the original operating agreement. Fix: include every amendment. An amendment you leave out can change who holds control.
  • Getting third-party certified and then bidding right away. Fix: finish the MySBA Certifications upload first.

How Long Does It Take to Get WOSB Certification?

SBA's rule says it will decide within 90 calendar days of receiving a complete package "whenever practicable." In practice, the clock starts only once SBA considers your file complete. Third-party timelines depend on the certifier.

PathPublished timelineSource
SBA (free)90 calendar days after a complete package, whenever practicable13 CFR 127.304
USWCC30–45 business days, starting after supporting documents are verifiedUSWCC
WBENC (with WBE)Typically 3–4 months for a new application: 30–60 days of documents and Q&A, 30 days of committee review, a 30-day site visit, then 1–2 weeks for the decisionWBEC East (WBENC partner)
SAM.gov activation (prerequisite)3–5 business days normally, currently several weeksWBENC

(Timelines as of October 2026; check each official page.)

SBA doesn't publish a live average processing time. Some private guides report waits of 6–8 months for SBA decisions, but those figures don't come from SBA (UnderstandMyCert), so treat 90 days as the best case. For example, if you're aiming at an agency's fourth-quarter buying season (July–September), submitting by the previous winter gives you room for a round of document requests.

If you're declined, you can reapply 90 days after the decline date. You'll need to have fixed every reason SBA gave, and SBA must give those reasons in writing (13 CFR 127.304). A decline costs you at least three months, so it's usually faster to send a complete package the first time.

To keep your certification, plan on a program examination every three years. SBA's annual attestation requirement is currently in abeyance, so you don't have to file an attestation every year (SBA). WBENC recommends submitting recertification 90 days before expiration (WBENC).

Free SBA Certification vs. Third-Party WOSB Certifier: Which Should You Choose?

For most applicants, SBA's free certification is the better pick: it costs nothing and it's what federal set-asides require. Third-party certifiers cost money and add a reviewer who answers to you. A WBE certificate also helps with corporate supplier programs. Self-certification ended on October 15, 2020, so none of these options is "self-certifying" (CRS R46322).

OptionCost (as of Oct 2026; check the official page)Covers EDWOSB?Who it suitsWho it's not for / limitation
SBA MySBA CertificationsFreeYesOwners whose documents are clean and who only need federal statusYou don't get a coach. You and SBA communicate through portal requests, and the 90-day target isn't guaranteed
USWCC$275 members / $350 non-members. One fee also covers its NWBE/IWBE certificatesYesBudget-minded owners who want an outside review with a published 30–45 business-day windowNot for anyone who needs a WBENC WBE for corporate buyers. You still have to file in MySBA (or pay for its CertificationPlus+ add-on) (USWCC)
NWBOC$400 for WOSB/EDWOSB, $700 combined with WBE. Annual renewal is $200 up to $2M in sales, $300 above thatYesOwners who want WOSB plus NWBOC's WBE in one applicationThe fee isn't refunded if you're denied or withdraw (NWBOC application)
WBENCWOSB is complimentary with a WBE application. WBE fees run $350 (under $1M) up to $1,250 ($50M+), plus 3% if you pay by credit card from July 1, 2026Not listed on WBENC's WOSB pageFirms selling to large corporations that ask for WBENC WBE statusNot for owners who only want federal status. You can only add WOSB during a new or recertifying WBE application, the process takes 3–4 months, and the fee is nonrefundable (WBENC; WBEC East)
El Paso Hispanic Chamber of CommerceCheck with the chamber directlyCheck directlyOwners in its regionSBA lists it as approved, but this guide couldn't find published fees or timelines

Decision tree

  1. Do corporate customers ask you for a WBE certificate? If yes, go with WBENC, or NWBOC's combined package, so one review produces both. If no, go to question 2.
  2. Do you qualify for EDWOSB? If yes, use SBA (free) or USWCC/NWBOC. All of them handle EDWOSB. If no, go to question 3.
  3. Are your operating agreement or bylaws clean, with no supermajority or unanimous-consent clauses favoring men and no outside job for the woman CEO? If yes, use SBA's free path. You'd be paying a fee for a review your documents don't need. If you aren't sure, fix the documents first (see the next section). A paid certifier reviews against the same Part 127 rules and can't approve documents that fail them.

No certifier can lower your risk of rejection by bending the rules. What a paid reviewer adds is structured follow-up. Your eligibility depends only on what your documents say.

Ownership and Control Documentation SBA Rejects Most Often

SBA declines applications over control clauses in operating agreements and bylaws, men who hold financial or signing power, and ownership percentages that don't match equity records. SBA doesn't publish decline statistics. The items below come from the specific rules applications are judged against in 13 CFR 127.201–127.202, along with the rule that inconsistent information leads to a decline.

1. Supermajority and unanimous-consent clauses

An LLC agreement might require approval from 75% of members or a unanimous vote to borrow money, sign contracts, or hire staff. If women own 60%, that clause gives the 40% male member veto power. Women must be the managing members "with control over all decisions" (13 CFR 127.202). The fix is to amend the agreement so ordinary and major business decisions need only a majority the women control. Keep the minority-protection votes, such as approving a sale of the whole company or a dissolution, limited to what's commercially standard.

2. A man holds the highest title or the real authority

Here's an example. The woman owner is "President," but her husband is "CEO," holds the line of credit, and is the only signer on the bank account. The rule requires that a woman hold the highest officer position and run day-to-day operations (13 CFR 127.202). To fix it, change the officer titles, add her as the primary signer on bank and credit accounts, and make sure board minutes or resolutions reflect the change.

3. The woman in charge has another full-time job

A W-2 from another employer in her personal tax return undercuts the requirement that she generally work full time during normal hours (13 CFR 127.202). Resolve it before you apply, or be ready to explain any part-time outside role in detail.

4. Ownership percentages that don't match across documents

The operating agreement says 51%, the K-1s show 50/50, and the SAM profile lists two equal owners. SBA declines applications when it can't determine eligibility because of inconsistent information (13 CFR Part 127, Subpart C). Put the stock ledger, operating agreement, K-1s, tax returns, and SAM record side by side, and correct the one that's wrong before you apply. Don't explain the mismatch afterward.

5. Indirect or conditional ownership

The usual problems are ownership held through a holding company, a trust where the woman isn't grantor, trustee, and sole beneficiary, a buy-sell agreement that triggers on a contingency, and voting rights assigned to someone else. Each one breaks the "unconditional and direct" requirement (13 CFR 127.201). The fix is to move the shares into the woman's own name and strip any conditions that don't follow normal commercial terms.

6. Distributions or pay that favor men

If distributions aren't at least 51% to the women, or a male employee earns more than the woman CEO without a justification, SBA reads the arrangement as control sitting elsewhere (13 CFR 127.201; 13 CFR 127.202). If a higher salary has a legitimate reason, such as a licensed professional's market rate, write that reason down.

7. Options and the stock ledger

Options held by men count as already exercised (13 CFR 127.201). For example, a woman owns 55% and a male partner holds options for another 10%. On a fully diluted basis she's at 50%, which fails. Recalculate on a fully diluted basis before you submit.

Next steps

Your first step is to check your NAICS code and SAM status today. Then compare your governing documents against the control rules before you open any application.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Look up your primary NAICS code on SBA's eligible NAICS list and confirm your SAM.gov registration is active.
  2. Print your operating agreement or bylaws and highlight every vote that needs more than a simple majority, every officer title, and every bank signer. Compare them against sections 1–3 above.
  3. Put your ownership percentages from the ledger, K-1s, and SAM side by side. If anything doesn't match, fix it before you sign in to MySBA Certifications.

If you'd rather not do it alone: APEX Accelerators are federally funded and offer free or low-cost help with SAM registration and certification paperwork. They suit first-time bidders who want someone to walk through the documents with them. They aren't the right choice if you need legal advice on restructuring an operating agreement. That's attorney work, and attorney fees vary widely. A paid third-party certifier such as USWCC ($275–$350) or NWBOC ($400) gives you a structured review (as of October 2026; check the official pages). It's not worth the fee if your documents are already clean and you only need federal status, because SBA's path is free.

Related guides on this site:

  • SAM.gov Registration Guide: 7 Steps From UEI to Active
  • 8(a) Certification Requirements: 2026 Pass/Fail Checklist, if you might qualify for both programs
  • SDVOSB Set Aside Requirements: 2026 Eligibility Checklist
  • Capability Statement Example: 5 Sections Buyers Read First, to put your new WOSB status in front of buyers

FAQ

What documents do I need for WOSB certification?

You'll need proof of U.S. citizenship for each qualifying woman, signed personal and business federal tax returns, and bank statements. Add your formation documents (articles, plus the operating agreement, bylaws and stock ledger, or partnership agreement) and any assumed-name or joint venture agreements (13 CFR Part 127, Subpart C). EDWOSB applicants also need three years of personal tax returns and a personal financial statement.

Is WOSB certification free?

Yes, when you apply through SBA at certifications.sba.gov. Third-party certifiers charge fees. USWCC charges $275–$350, NWBOC charges $400, and WBENC includes WOSB with WBE fees of $350–$1,250 (as of October 2026; check the official pages).

What is the difference between WOSB and EDWOSB?

EDWOSB adds three personal financial limits for each woman owner on top of the WOSB ownership and control rules. Her net worth must be under $850,000, her three-year average AGI must be $400,000 or less, and her total assets must be $6.5 million or less (13 CFR 127.203). EDWOSBs can also compete in the 113 NAICS codes reserved for EDWOSB set-asides, a figure from SBA's March 2022 list.

Does WOSB certification expire?

Certified firms go through a program examination every three years. SBA's annual attestation requirement is currently in abeyance (SBA). Third-party certifiers have their own renewal cycles. NWBOC, for example, charges an annual renewal fee.

Can I self-certify as WOSB?

No. Self-certification for WOSB set-asides ended on October 15, 2020 (CRS R46322). You now need certification from SBA or an approved third-party certifier, and it has to appear in MySBA Certifications.

item.title: RFQ vs RFP: 5 FAR Clues and What to Submit (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: RFQ vs RFP in federal contracting: the FAR clauses, thresholds and solicitation wording that show which one you're reading, and exactly what to submit.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

An RFQ (Request for Quotation) asks for your price on a requirement the government has already defined. An RFP (Request for Proposal) asks for a technical approach as well as a price, and the agency judges both against stated evaluation factors. To tell them apart in a federal solicitation, check the FAR provisions it cites and the word it uses for your response. The two also differ legally in what happens after you submit, which the definitions section below covers.

Which option is right for you?

The quickest way to decide is to match your situation to the notice type on SAM.gov and open the document that controls your response.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, never bid beforeRFQs under $350,000 for a product or service you already sell, because pricing against a fixed spec is easier than writing a full proposalThe notice's "Attachments/Links" section on SAM.gov, then the instructions provision (52.212-1)
Daily bidding, small teamCombined Synopsis/Solicitations for commercial work, because the whole solicitation is one notice with short deadlinesThe FAR 12.603 statement at the top of the notice that names IFB, RFQ or RFP
Established firm with past performanceRFPs where Section M weights past performance, since that's where your track record countsSection L (instructions) and Section M (evaluation factors) per FAR 15.204-1
Tight budget, no proposal writerRFIs and Sources Sought notices, because a capability statement costs little to write and can influence a set-asideOur Sources Sought response template
Not yet registeredNeither until registration is done, because FAR 4.1102 requires SAM registration when you submit an offer or quotationOur SAM.gov registration guide

What Is RFQ and RFP? (The Core Definitions)

Beyond the price-versus-approach difference, the FAR draws a legal line between the two, and it affects you after you hit submit.

FAR 2.101 defines "offer" this way: responses to invitations for bids are "bids," responses to requests for proposals are "proposals," and responses to requests for quotations "are 'quotations,' not offers." FAR 13.004 explains the effect: "A quotation is not an offer and, consequently, cannot be accepted by the Government to form a binding contract." If the government issues an order based on your quote, the order is the government's offer. A contract exists only once you accept it, either in writing or by delivering or substantially performing the work.

Dollar thresholds decide which method an agency can use. As of October 2026, FAR 2.101 sets these values:

Threshold (FAR 2.101, as of Oct 2026)Amount
Micro-purchase threshold (base)$15,000
Micro-purchase, construction subject to wage requirements$2,000
Micro-purchase, services subject to labor standards$2,500
Simplified acquisition threshold (SAT)$350,000
SAT, domestic contingency/emergency$1,000,000

FAR 13.003 tells agencies to use simplified acquisition procedures "to the maximum extent practicable" for purchases at or below the SAT, and an RFQ is the standard tool for those purchases. Above that level, and for complex buys, agencies usually switch to FAR Part 15 negotiation and the RFP.

A 2026 wrinkle: the FAR overhaul

Under the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul (RFO), many agencies now follow class deviations that differ from the codified FAR. The RFO Part 12 deviation text tells agencies to issue "a request for quotations (RFQ) followed by a purchase order" for commercial acquisitions up to $9 million ($15 million in certain emergencies). Above $9 million, agencies use Part 15 RFPs or Part 14 invitations for bids, and the deviation says "Use of an RFP is the preferred method because it includes consideration of past performance." The RFO Part 13 deviation narrows Part 13 to noncommercial buys at or below the SAT. Proposed rules covering Parts 12, 13 and 15 (FAR Case 2026-003) had a comment deadline of October 19, 2026, according to the SBA Office of Advocacy. The practical result: a commercial RFQ can now be much larger than $350,000. Go by the clauses each solicitation actually cites, not by older rules of thumb.

What Is RFQ and RFP in Procurement? How the FAR Actually Labels Them

In federal procurement, the clauses cited inside the document tell you the solicitation type more reliably than the title on the cover. Agencies reuse forms and templates, so a "Request for Quote" header can sit on a document that cites Part 15 evaluation language, and the reverse also happens.

Here are five clues, in the order to check them.

  1. The statement at the top of a combined notice. FAR 12.603(c)(2) requires "a statement that the solicitation is issued as an invitation to bid (IFB), request for quotation (RFQ) or request for proposal (RFP)." Use the Find command (Ctrl+F) to search for those three acronyms.
  2. The noun used for your response. Search for "quotation," "quoter," "proposal" and "offeror." A document that asks for "quotations" from "quoters" is using simplified acquisition. One that asks for "proposals" from "offerors" and mentions a "competitive range" or "discussions" is using Part 15 negotiation.
  3. The instructions provision. 52.212-1 (Instructions to Offerors—Commercial Products and Commercial Services) appears in commercial solicitations of every kind. 52.215-1 (Instructions to Offerors—Competitive Acquisition) signals a Part 15 negotiated procurement. If you see 52.212-1 together with an addendum that adds Part 15-style volumes, prepare a proposal.
  4. How evaluation is described. For simplified buys, FAR 13.106-1 only requires the agency to state "the basis on which award will be made (price alone or price and other factors, e.g., past performance and quality)." An RFP under FAR 15.203 must list "factors and significant subfactors that will be used to evaluate the proposal and their relative importance." A ranked list of factors with relative weights means RFP.
  5. The estimated value and the form. Under FAR 13.307, simplified acquisitions use the SF 1449 or the SF 18 (Request for Quotations). If the estimate is clearly above the threshold that applies (the $350,000 SAT, or $9 million for commercial buys under the RFO deviation) and you can't find simplified-procedure language, assume Part 15.

Example (illustrative): Suppose a notice is titled "RFQ – Janitorial Services," cites 52.212-1, and says award goes to "the lowest-priced technically acceptable quote." That is an RFQ, and your package is a price plus proof that you meet the specs. Now suppose a notice is titled "Janitorial Services," cites 52.215-1, and says "technical approach is significantly more important than price." That is an RFP, even though the work is the same.

What Is RFI vs RFP? Where the Information Request Fits First

An RFI is market research. You submit nothing binding and no award follows. FAR 15.201(e) says RFIs "may be used when the Government does not presently intend to award a contract, but wants to obtain price, delivery, other market information, or capabilities for planning purposes," and adds that responses are not offers.

RFI / Sources SoughtRFP
PurposeShape the requirement, test the market, decide on a set-asideSelect a contractor
What you sendCapability statement, answers to questions, comments on draft specsTechnical, management, past performance and price volumes
Binding?NoYes
SAM.gov notice typeSources Sought (code "r") or Special Notice ("s")Solicitation ("o") or Combined Synopsis/Solicitation ("k") (GSA Opportunities API)
Main payoff for a small businessCan lead the agency to set the buy asideContract award

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Sending a 40-page proposal to an RFI. Reviewers are looking for capability and interest, not pricing tables. Fix: answer only the questions asked and lead with a concise capability statement. Our capability statement example shows which sections buyers read first.
  • Skipping RFIs because "there's no contract." Agencies use the responses to decide whether enough small businesses can do the work. Fix: if you could realistically perform the work, respond and state your size status under the notice's NAICS code. Our guide to SBA size standards by NAICS explains how to check it.
  • Quoting firm prices in an RFI. Fix: give ranges or mark figures as rough order of magnitude (ROM) for planning only.

What Is RFI and RFP Process? The Typical Sequence in Federal Contracting

A typical sequence runs from Sources Sought or RFI, to presolicitation or draft RFP, to final RFP, then proposals, evaluation and award. New bidders often switch into proposal mode while the agency is still at the RFI stage.

FAR 15.201(c) lists the early-exchange tools agencies may use: industry conferences, one-on-one meetings, presolicitation notices, draft RFPs, RFIs, preproposal conferences and site visits. FAR 10.002 separately lists market research techniques, including "interchange meetings or holding presolicitation conferences."

Here is how the timing works under FAR 5.203:

  1. Sources Sought / RFI (optional). There's no minimum response time in 5.203, so these can close within days.
  2. Presolicitation notice. For most actions it must be published "at least 15 days before issuance of a solicitation." Contracting officers can set shorter periods for commercial buys.
  3. Solicitation (RFP or RFQ). For acquisitions above the SAT, the minimum response time is 30 days from issuance. Research and development requires at least 45 days. For commercial buys over $25,000, the contracting officer sets a "reasonable" time.
  4. Questions and amendments. Amendments arrive as SF 30 modifications (FAR 13.307 lists the SF 30), and you must acknowledge each one. 52.212-1(b) lists "acknowledgment of solicitation amendments" as a required item.
  5. Evaluation and award. The default under 52.215-1(f)(4) is award without discussions, so the government expects your best terms in the first submission.
  6. Award Notice (SAM.gov notice type "a").

To follow one opportunity through these stages on SAM.gov:

  1. Go to SAM.gov, select Search, and choose the Contract Opportunities domain.
  2. In the Notice Type filter, pick Sources Sought and Presolicitation for early work, or Solicitation and Combined Synopsis/Solicitation for live bids.
  3. Add your NAICS Code and Set Aside filters.
  4. Open a notice and select Follow so that new versions and amendments under the same notice ID are easy to track.
  5. Read the Description and every file under Attachments/Links. The FAR clauses are usually in the attachments, not the summary.

Pitfall: treating a Combined Synopsis/Solicitation like a presolicitation. Under FAR 12.603, the notice states "This announcement constitutes the only solicitation." No second document is coming, and the clock is already running.

What Is RFI and RFP in Sales? How Commercial Usage Differs From Federal Rules

In private-sector sales, buyers use RFI, RFQ and RFP loosely, and no regulation like the FAR fixes what each one means. A federal response strategy won't carry over unchanged.

The FAR is the federal baseline. It defines who is making an offer (FAR 2.101), how late submissions are handled (52.212-1 and 52.215-1), and what an RFP must disclose about evaluation (FAR 15.203). A corporate procurement team follows its own policy and its own contract terms.

Example (illustrative): A hospital system's "RFP" might be a two-page spreadsheet of unit prices, which functions as an RFQ. Its "RFI" might include a pricing tab it later holds you to. A company's purchasing department might negotiate with two finalists after a "final" deadline, a step the FAR's late-proposal rules would generally bar in a federal acquisition.

Pitfalls when moving between the two worlds

  • Assuming commercial flexibility applies in federal bids. A federal proposal that misses the deadline is usually rejected. 52.212-1 allows only narrow exceptions, such as an electronic submission received by 5:00 p.m. one working day before the deadline, or the only proposal received. Fix: plan your upload to finish a day early.
  • Assuming federal protections apply in commercial deals. Without a FAR-style evaluation section, a private buyer may never tell you how price was weighed. Fix: ask in writing how the decision will be made before you invest heavily.
  • Reusing a sales deck as a federal technical volume. Fix: rebuild it to match the solicitation's instructions section by section.

What Is RFI, RFQ and RFP? Comparing All Three Side by Side

Seen together, the three differ most in where they sit in the FAR, how large the buy can be, and how much the agency must tell you about evaluation.

RFIRFQRFP
FAR home15.201(e), Part 10Part 13 (simplified); Part 12 under the RFO deviationPart 15 (15.203)
Your response is calledResponse / informationQuotationProposal
Legally an offer?NoNo (FAR 13.004)Yes (FAR 2.101)
Typical value range (as of Oct 2026)AnyUp to $350,000 SAT; up to $9M for commercial under the RFO Part 12 deviationAny, typical for complex or higher-value buys
Evaluation disclosureNoneBasis of award (price alone or price plus other factors) per 13.106-1Factors, subfactors and relative importance
Typical formsNotice text onlySF 18 or SF 1449 (13.307)Uniform contract format Sections A–M (15.204-1)

Example (illustrative): An agency that needs 200 ruggedized laptops might post an RFI asking which models meet a draft spec. Once the spec is fixed, it could post an RFQ asking for unit price and delivery date. If it later decides it needs a vendor to design, deploy and support a field computing system, that is an RFP, because the agency is now comparing approaches.

What Is the Difference Between RFQ and RFP in What You Must Submit?

Day to day, the difference shows up in the paperwork: an RFQ package is mostly a priced quote plus required representations, while an RFP package is a set of separate volumes laid out exactly as Section L instructs.

ItemRFQ (commercial, 52.212-1)RFP (Part 15, 52.215-1 + Section L)
Solicitation number, deadline, contact infoRequired (52.212-1(b))Required on the first page (52.215-1(c)(2))
Technical content"Technical description" sufficient to evaluateFull technical/management volume per Section L
Price"Price and any discount terms"Separate price or cost volume, often with supporting data
Past performanceOnly when it's an evaluation factorUsually its own volume
Reps & certsCompleted per 52.212-3Section K
Signature authorityNot separately specified in 52.212-1(b)Authorized signatory; agents need "evidence of that agent's authority"
How long your price stays valid30 calendar days default (52.212-1)Days stated on the cover sheet, unless you propose otherwise

Sources: 52.212-1, 52.215-1, 15.204-1.

Steps to build the right package

  1. Search the solicitation for "52.212-1" and "52.215-1" and note any "Addendum to 52.212-1." Addenda often add page limits and volumes.
  2. In an RFP, copy every "shall" sentence from Section L (or the addendum) into a compliance checklist, one row per sentence. Then copy the factors from Section M next to it so your headings match how evaluators score.
  3. Confirm the set-aside type and your size under the NAICS code. If you're unsure how a partial set-aside changes who can win which part, read our total vs partial set-aside checklist.
  4. Price exactly the line items listed in Section B or the SF 1449 schedule. Don't merge or rename CLINs.
  5. Acknowledge every amendment and submit through the method the solicitation names.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Adding marketing material to an RFQ. If award is on price alone, extra pages don't score. Fix: send the price, the spec confirmations and the required forms.
  • Leaving out a past performance volume in an RFP. Fix: when Section M lists past performance, follow the format and number of references Section L asks for. If you have no federal history, include relevant commercial work when the instructions allow it.
  • Writing "pricing valid 15 days" when the solicitation asks for 30 or more. Fix: match or exceed the acceptance period in the solicitation.
  • Assuming you can fix the proposal later. 52.215-1 states the government intends to award without discussions. Fix: submit your best price and approach the first time.

RFQ vs RFP vs RFI vs RFT vs RFB vs Tender: One Comparison Table

RFT and "tender" are used mainly outside the U.S. and correspond most closely to a U.S. RFP or invitation for bids. RFB overlaps with sealed bidding under FAR Part 14. Map each term back to the closest FAR method before deciding what to send.

The UK's Procurement Act 2023, for example, describes awarding contracts to the supplier with "the most advantageous tender in a competitive tendering procedure" (section 19). In the FAR, the formal term for a bid request is "invitation for bids" (IFB). Under FAR 14.101, bids "shall be evaluated without discussions," are "publicly opened," and award goes to the responsible bidder whose conforming bid is most advantageous "considering only price and the price-related factors."

TermWhere you'll see itClosest FAR methodYour responseDiscussions?
RFIFederal, commercialMarket research (15.201(e))Information onlyN/A
RFQFederal, commercialSimplified acquisition (Part 13; Part 12 under RFO)Quotation (not an offer)Not a formal stage
RFPFederal, commercialNegotiation (Part 15)Proposal (offer)Possible, but default is none (52.215-1(f)(4))
IFB / RFBFederal (IFB), state/local (RFB)Sealed bidding (Part 14)Sealed bid (offer)No (14.101)
RFT / TenderUK, Australia, Canada, EUUsually Part 15 or Part 14, depending on whether quality is scoredTenderDepends on that country's rules

All FAR citations above refer to the codified FAR text as shown on acquisition.gov when checked in October 2026.

Next steps

You can do the first round of this work yourself today, starting with one real notice.

DIY actions for today

  1. If you don't have an active SAM.gov registration yet, start it now. FAR 4.1102 requires it at the time you submit an offer or quotation. Our SAM.gov registration guide walks through the steps.
  2. On SAM.gov, filter Contract Opportunities by your NAICS code and Notice Type = Combined Synopsis/Solicitation. Open three notices and run the five clue checks from the section on how the FAR labels RFQs and RFPs. Write down whether each one is an RFQ or an RFP and which provision told you.
  3. Find one Sources Sought notice in your NAICS code and respond with a two-page capability statement using our Sources Sought template.

If you'd rather not do it alone

  • APEX Accelerators: free. These centers operate under a Department of Defense cooperative agreement and offer counseling at no cost, including bid reviews and registration help (Washington APEX Accelerator; DC APEX Accelerator). Good for first-time bidders who want someone to check their reading of a solicitation. Not ideal if you need someone to write a 50-page proposal for you. Counselors advise rather than ghostwrite, and availability varies by location.
  • Independent proposal writers or consultants: paid. There is no official rate card, so ask for a fixed written quote per solicitation (as of October 2026; check each firm's current terms). This can make sense for a firm chasing a large RFP with a short deadline. It's usually a poor fit for RFQs, where the package is mostly your price and can be done in-house. Before you sign, keep in mind that the consultant can't supply past performance you don't have.

Related guides on this site

  • Capability Statement Example: 5 Sections Buyers Read First

FAQ

What is RFQ RFP process timeline for a typical federal solicitation?

For acquisitions above the simplified acquisition threshold, FAR 5.203 generally requires a notice at least 15 days before the solicitation and at least 30 days to respond after it's issued (45 days for R&D). Commercial buys can have shorter, "reasonable" response times set by the contracting officer. RFQs under the SAT often close in days, so check the response date on every notice.

Can an RFQ turn into an RFP if the agency changes its requirement?

An agency can cancel an RFQ and reissue the requirement as an RFP, or amend the solicitation, if the requirement or estimated value changes. For example, the RFO Part 12 deviation moves commercial buys over $9 million to Part 15 or Part 14. Follow the notice on SAM.gov and read each amendment for changes to the cited provisions.

Is a response to an RFQ legally binding like a bid under sealed bidding?

No. Unlike a sealed bid, a quotation is not an offer (FAR 13.004); see the core definitions section above for how a contract forms from an order. Even so, quote only prices you're prepared to honor.

Do I need a SAM.gov registration to respond to either an RFQ or RFP?

Yes, in most cases. FAR 4.1102 says "Offerors and quoters are required to be registered in SAM at the time an offer or quotation is submitted." Exceptions are narrow, such as certain micro-purchases paid by government purchase card and some classified or urgent actions.

item.title: SBA Size Standards by NAICS: 2026 Table, Steps & Appeals
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: SBA size standards by NAICS code: current caps for 20+ codes, how to pick a code when you span industries, and how it decides set-aside eligibility.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The SBA sets a size standard for each NAICS code. It's the largest your company can be, measured in average annual receipts or in employees, and still count as "small" for a contract classified under that code. To check it, find the 6-digit NAICS code on the solicitation, look that code up in the SBA's Table of Size Standards (the version in effect since March 17, 2023), and compare the cap with your company-wide receipts or headcount, including affiliates (SBA, SBA table). A firm can be small under one code and "other than small" under another. That means the code on each solicitation decides which set-asides you can bid on, not the code you like best.

Which option is right for you?

Start with the question that fits your situation, and open the first page listed in the table.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, not registered yetLook up 3–6 NAICS codes that describe what you actually sell, and choose a primary codeCensus NAICS search
Registered in SAM.gov, bidding regularlyCheck your size against the NAICS code on each solicitation before you write the proposal13 CFR 121.201 size table
Your work spans several industriesRank your codes by the receipts or headcount behind them, and note where you're small and where you aren'tSBA Table of Size Standards (Excel)
Growing fast and close to a capWork out your 5-year receipts average or 24-month employee average now13 CFR 121.104
Tight budget, want a second opinionFree counseling from an APEX Accelerator before you pay anyoneAPEX Accelerators
You think a solicitation has the wrong codeDraft a NAICS code appeal within 10 calendar days13 CFR 121.1103

Why these picks: beginners need accurate codes before anything else. Active bidders lose the most when they misjudge size on a single solicitation. Multi-industry firms are the ones most likely to be small under one code and large under another.

What Are SBA Size Standards by NAICS Code?

SBA size standards by NAICS code set the maximum average annual receipts or employee count a firm can have to be "small" in that industry. The SBA says that size standards "define the largest size a business can be to participate in government contracting programs," and that most manufacturers with 500 or fewer employees and most non-manufacturers with average annual receipts under $7.5 million qualify as small, though many industries have higher limits (SBA).

Each standard is attached to a 6-digit code from the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS). The regulation that lists them all is 13 CFR 121.201. The SBA publishes the same data as a PDF and an Excel file. The table version in effect as of October 2026 is dated March 17, 2023 (SBA table page). The SBA counts 995 separate size standards today (Mayer Brown).

Three rules apply to every code:

  • The cap is company-wide. You measure the whole business against the cap, plus every affiliate. The SBA says you "must include the employees or receipts of all affiliates" (SBA). You don't split your revenue by NAICS code.
  • Some codes have exceptions. For example, 541330 Engineering Services has a $25.5 million cap, but its exception for military and aerospace equipment and military weapons is $47.0 million (13 CFR 121.201).
  • Each contract carries one code. The contracting officer assigns one NAICS code and its size standard to each solicitation, contract and order (FAR 19.102).

How to Find Your NAICS Code and Matching Size Standard

First find the NAICS code that best matches each product or service you sell. Then look up that code in the SBA table to get the employee or receipts cap. The SBA notes that a business "will generally have a primary NAICS code, but it can also have multiple NAICS codes if it sells multiple products and services" (SBA).

Step-by-step lookup

  1. Search the Census NAICS tool. Go to census.gov/naics, type a plain keyword into the NAICS search box (for example, "janitorial" or "software"), and choose the 2022 NAICS year. That's the edition behind the current SBA table. Open each result and read the full description, including the "cross-references" that tell you which activities belong somewhere else.
  2. Write down every code that fits real revenue. For each candidate code, ask whether you've actually earned money from that work or can show past performance in it. Leave out codes you're only hoping to grow into.
  3. Get the cap. Download the Excel version of the SBA Table of Size Standards and filter the NAICS column for your codes. The PDF and 13 CFR 121.201 contain the same numbers. Check the footnotes for exceptions.
  4. Run the SBA tool as a cross-check. The SBA Size Standards Tool asks "Do you qualify as a small business for government contracting purposes?" and walks you through code and size inputs. It gives you a quick answer, not a formal determination.
  5. Enter the codes in SAM.gov. In your entity registration, add the codes and choose a primary NAICS. When you select at least one small business code, SAM.gov asks for Size Metrics (receipts and employees) and uses them to show your size status for each code (SAM.gov entity checklist). If you aren't registered yet, follow our SAM.gov registration guide.

Common mistakes and fixes

  • Mistake: using a code from your state license or tax return without checking it. Fix: read the Census definition. A code that's close enough for tax purposes can carry a very different cap.
  • Mistake: reading the 4- or 5-digit industry group. Fix: size standards attach to the 6-digit code (and sometimes to an exception under it). Always check all six digits.
  • Mistake: using an old PDF of the table. Fix: confirm that the file name or header says "Effective March 17, 2023," or a later date if the SBA issues a new final rule.

SBA Size Standards by NAICS Code: Employees vs. Revenue Table

Manufacturing and wholesale codes mostly use employee caps. Services, construction and retail codes mostly use average annual receipts. The numbers below come from 13 CFR 121.201 as of October 2026. Check the official page before you bid, because a proposed overhaul is pending (covered below).
